nodes.name: Goodman's multi-color monochromatic triangle question
nodes.statement: Subsequently, in~\cite{Goodman_1985}, he also asked for an answer to the natural generalization of this problem to more than two colors.
nodes.statement_short: Determine the minimum fraction of monochromatic triangles in edge-colorings of $K_n$ with more than two colors.

nodes.name: Cummings et al. three-color Ramsey multiplicity of triangles
nodes.statement: It took over 50 years and the advent of flag algebras for even the case of three colors to be settled: Cummings et al.~\cite{CummingsEtAl_2013} showed that asymptotically at least a $1/25$ fraction of all triangles need to be monochromatic in any three-edge-coloring of $K_n$.
nodes.statement_short: At least a 1/25 fraction of triangles are monochromatic in any 3-edge-coloring of $K_n$, asymptotically.
conclusions: asymptotically at least a $1/25$ fraction of all triangles need to be monochromatic in any three-edge-coloring of $K_n$

nodes.name: Four-color Ramsey multiplicity of triangles
nodes.statement: Asymptotically at least a $1/256$ fraction of all triangles are monochromatic in any four-edge-coloring of $K_n$ and any sufficiently large extremal coloring must be based on one of the two $R(3,3,3)$ Ramsey-colorings of $K_{16}$.
nodes.statement_short: $m_4(3)=1/256$, and large extremal colorings are blow-ups of one of the two $R(3,3,3)$ Ramsey colorings of $K_{16}$.
conclusions: Asymptotically at least a $1/256$ fraction of all triangles are monochromatic in any four-edge-coloring of $K_n$
any sufficiently large extremal coloring must be based on one of the two $R(3,3,3)$ Ramsey-colorings of $K_{16}$
nodes.label: thm:fourcolortriangles

nodes.name: c-coloring
nodes.statement: We are studying the family of $c$-colorings of the edges between a finite number of vertices, that is maps $G: \big\{ \{u, v\} \mid u,v \in V, \,  u \neq v \big\} \to [c] = \{1, \ldots, c\}$ where $V$ is any finite set.

nodes.name: Vertex set and order
nodes.statement: Following common notation for graphs, we write $V(G) = V$ for the \emph{set of vertices} of such a coloring $G$ as well as $v(G) = |V(G)|$ for its \emph{order}.

nodes.name: Color class E_i(G)
nodes.statement: We also write $E_i(G) = G^{-1} (\{i\})$ for the set of edges colored with color $i \in [c]$.

nodes.name: Set of colorings G^(c)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G}^{(c)}$ denote the set of all such colorings and $\mathcal{G}_n^{(c)}$ the set of all colorings of order $n$.

nodes.name: Isomorphic colorings
nodes.statement: Two colorings $G, G' \in \mathcal{G}^{(c)}$ are \emph{isomorphic}, written as $G \simeq G'$, if there exists a bijection $\varphi: V(G) \overset{\sim}{\hookrightarrow} V(G')$ such that $G \equiv G' \circ \varphi$.

nodes.name: Restriction G[S]
nodes.statement: Given $G \in \mathcal{G}^{(c)}$ and $S \subseteq V(G)$, we write $G[S]$ for the restriction of $G$ to edges between vertices in $S$.

nodes.name: Sub-coloring and copy
nodes.statement: We say $H$ is a \emph{sub-coloring} of $G$ if there exists a \emph{copy} of $H$ in $G$, that is if there exists $S \subseteq V(G)$ s.t. $G[S] \simeq H$.

nodes.name: Density p(H;G)
nodes.statement: Given colorings $H \in \mathcal{G}_k^{(c)}$ and $G \in \mathcal{G}_n^{(c)}$, we write $p(H; G) = |\{ S \subseteq V(G) \mid G[S] \simeq H\}| / {n \choose k}$ for the \emph{density} of $H$ in $G$.

nodes.name: Ramsey's theorem (multi-color)
nodes.statement_short: The multi-color Ramsey number $R(t_1,\ldots,t_c)$ is finite; also introduces $K_t^i$.

nodes.name: Diagonal Ramsey number R_c(t)
nodes.statement: For the diagonal case, where $t_1 = \ldots = t_c$, we write $R_c(t) = R(t, \ldots, t)$.

nodes.name: Ramsey multiplicity problem
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the total density of monochromatic $K_t$ over $c$-colorings of $K_n$; defines $m_c(t;n)$.

nodes.name: Ramsey multiplicity limit m_c(t)
nodes.statement: A simple double-counting argument, see \cref{lemma:double_counting} in the next section, establishes that $m_c(t; n)$ is monotonically increasing, so that the limit $m_c(t) = \lim_{n \to \infty} m_c(t; n)$ is well defined and satisfies $m_c(t) \geq m_c(t; n)$ for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: $m_c(t;n)$ is monotone, so $m_c(t)=\lim_n m_c(t;n)$ exists and bounds every $m_c(t;n)$.

nodes.name: Positivity of m_c(t)
nodes.statement: Note that $m_c(t; n) > 0$ as long as $n \geq R_c(t)$ and therefore $m_c(t) > 0$ by Ramsey's theorem.

nodes.name: Probabilistic upper bound on m_c(t)
nodes.statement_short: A uniformly random coloring gives $m_c(t)\le c^{1-\binom t2}$.

nodes.name: Probabilistic upper bound (2.1)
nodes.statement: m_c(t) \leq c^{1 - {t \choose 2}}.
nodes.label: eq:prob_upper

nodes.name: Looped coloring
nodes.statement: Another way to obtain an upper bound is by blowing up a coloring of the edges of a \emph{looped} complete graph, that is a map $C: \big\{ \{u, v\} \mid u, v \in V \big\} \to [c]$.

nodes.name: Set of looped colorings L^(c)
nodes.statement: We use the same notation concerning the vertex and edge set as we did for unlooped colorings and write $\mathcal{L}^{(c)}$ for the set of all such colorings as well as $\mathcal{L}_n^{(c)}$ for colorings of order $n$.

nodes.name: Embedding into a looped coloring
nodes.statement: A coloring $H \in \mathcal{G}^{(c)}$ \emph{embeds} into a given $C \in \mathcal{L}^{(c)}_k$, if there exists a (not necessarily injective) map $\varphi: V(H) \to V(C)$ satisfying $H( \{u, v \} ) = C ( \{ \varphi(u), \varphi(v) \})$ for all  $u, v \in V(H)$.

nodes.name: Family of blow-up colorings B(C)
nodes.statement: We now let $\mathcal{B} (C) = \{ H \in \mathcal{G}^{(c)} \mid H \text{ embeds into } C \}$ denote the \emph{family of blow-up colorings} of $C$.

nodes.name: Weighted family of blow-up colorings
nodes.statement: Given some probability vector $\mathbf{w} = (w_v)_{v\in V(C)}$, that is $w_v \geq 0$ for $v \in V(C)$ and $\sum_{v\in V(C)}w_v = 1$, we additionally write $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbf{w}} (C)$ for the \emph{weighted family of blow-up colorings} of $C$, that is the set of all elements in $\mathcal{B} (C)$ for which $\varphi$ can be chosen such that $\big| |\varphi^{-1}(\{v\})| - w_v \cdot v(G) \big| \leq 1$ for all $v\in V(C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Blow-ups of $C$ whose part sizes follow the probability vector $\mathbf w$ up to rounding.

nodes.name: Weighted embedding density
Blow-up upper bound
nodes.statement:
Given any $C \in \mathcal{L}^{(c)}_k$ and a probability vector $\mathbf{w}$ for $C$, we have 
    \[
        m_c(t) \leq \hat{p}(K_t^1; C, \mathbf{w}) + \ldots + \hat{p}(K_t^c; C, \mathbf{w}).
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Any weighted looped coloring gives an upper bound on $m_c(t)$ via its monochromatic embedding densities.
nodes.label: lemma:blowup

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: Clearly $m_c(t) \leq \lim_{n \to \infty} \min_{G \in \mathcal{G}_n^{(c)} \cap \mathcal{B}_{\mathbf{w}}(C)} p(K_t^1; G) + \ldots + p(K_t^c; G)$, so the statement follows by observing that, asymptotically as $n$ tends to infinity, $p(H;G) = \hat{p}(H; C, \mathbf{w}) + o(1)$ for any $H \in \mathcal{G}^{(c)}$ and $G \in \mathcal{G}_n^{(c)} \cap \mathcal{B}_{\mathbf{w}}(C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the minimum to weighted blow-ups and use that their densities converge to the embedding densities.

nodes.name: Ramsey construction upper bound
nodes.statement:
In our case, the most relevant candidates for colorings $C$ that can be used in \cref{lemma:blowup} are obtained by considering a Ramsey-coloring on $r = R_{c-1}(t) - 1$ vertices avoiding cliques of size $t$ in any of the $c-1$ colors. Coloring the loops with the additional $c$-th color and using the uniform weighting $\mathbf{1 / r} = (1/r, \ldots, 1/r)$, this implies an upper bound of

\begin{equation} m_c(t) \leq (R_{c-1}(t) - 1)^{1-t},
\end{equation}

see also Theorem 5.2 in~\cite{fox2008there}.
nodes.statement_short: Blowing up an $R_{c-1}(t)$-Ramsey coloring with loops in color $c$ gives $m_c(t)\le (R_{c-1}(t)-1)^{1-t}$.

nodes.name: Goodman's theorem
nodes.statement:
m_2(3; n) \cdot {n \choose 3} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
        2 {u \choose 3} & \text{if } n = 2u,\\
        \frac{2}{3} u (u-1) (4u+1) & \text{if } n = 4u+1,\\
        \frac{2}{3} u (u+1) (4u-1) & \text{if } n = 4u+3,
        \end{array}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Exact minimum number of monochromatic triangles in a 2-edge-coloring of $K_n$, by residue of $n$ mod 4.

nodes.name: Erdős' conjecture on Ramsey multiplicity
nodes.statement: Given that the former bound dominates when $t$ grows as long as $c = 2$, Erd\H{o}s suggested~\cite{Erdos_1962} that the probabilistic upper bound should always be tight in this case.
nodes.statement_short: For two colors the random-coloring bound $m_2(t)=2^{1-\binom t2}$ should be tight.

nodes.name: Thomason's disproof of Erdős' conjecture
nodes.statement: This was disproven by Thomason~\cite{Thomason_1989} for any $t \geq 4$ and a significant number of results since then have tried to either determine improved asymptotics for $m_2(t)$ or specific values of it for small $t$~\cite{Conlon_2012,deza2012conjecture,even2015note,Franek_2002,FranekRodl_1993,Giraud_1979,GrzesikEtAl_2020,jagger1996multiplicities,Niess_2012,Sawin_2021,Sperfeld_2011,Thomason_1997, Wolf_2010,ParczykEtAl_2022}.

nodes.name: Value of m_2(4)
nodes.statement: As of now, even $m_2(4)$ remains open, with the best current lower and upper bounds of $0.0296 \leq m_2(4) \leq 0.03014$ respectively due to Grzesik et al.~\cite{GrzesikEtAl_2020} as well as Parczyk et al.~\cite{ParczykEtAl_2022}.
nodes.origin_citation: Grzesik et al. 2020; Parczyk et al. 2022

nodes.name: Asymptotic bounds on m_2(t) (Conlon; Jagger-Stovicek-Thomason)
nodes.statement: For the asymptotic values, there has likewise been scarce progress, with the current best lower bound of $C^{-t^2 (1 + o(1))} \leq m_2(t)$ for $C \approx 2.18$ due to Conlon~\cite{Conlon_2012} and the best upper bound of $m_2(t) \leq 0.835 \cdot 2^{1-{t\choose 2}}$ for $t \geq 7$ due to Jagger, {\v{S}}{\'t}ov{\'\i}{\v{c}}ek, and Thomason~\cite{jagger1996multiplicities}.

nodes.name: Coloring C_R(3,3)
nodes.statement: In order to state their result in its fullest strength, let $C_{R(3,3)}$ denote the coloring in $\mathcal{L}^{(3)}_{5}$ obtained by taking the unique Ramsey $2$-coloring of a complete graph on five vertices that avoids monochromatic triangles and coloring the loops with the third color, that is $E_1 (C_{R(3,3)} )$ and $E_2 (C_{R(3,3)} )$ both are $5$-cycles and $E_3 (C_{R(3,3)} )$ contains all five loops.

nodes.name: Extremal three-color family G^(3)_ex
nodes.statement:
Let 
$\mathcal{G}^{(3)}_\textrm{ex} \subset \mathcal{G}^{(3)}$ now consist of all colorings that can be obtained by (i) selecting an element in $\mathcal{B}_\mathbf{1/5} (C_{R(3,3)} )$, (ii) recoloring some of the edges from the first or second color to instead use the third color without creating any additional monochromatic triangles, and (iii) applying any permutation of the colors.
nodes.statement_short: Colorings from balanced blow-ups of $C_{R(3,3)}$, recolored into the third color without new triangles, up to color permutation.

nodes.name: Cummings et al. characterization of extremal three-colorings
nodes.statement:
There exists an $n_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that any 
    element in $\mathcal{G}_n^{(3)}$ of order $n \geq n_0$ minimizing the number of monochromatic triangles must be in $\mathcal{G}^{(3)}_\textrm{ex}$.
assumptions: any element in $\mathcal{G}_n^{(3)}$ of order $n \geq n_0$ minimizing the number of monochromatic triangles

nodes.name: Colorings C'_R(3,3,3) and C''_R(3,3,3)
nodes.statement: Let $C'_{R(3,3,3)}$ and $C''_{R(3,3,3)}$ denote the two colorings in $\mathcal{L}^{(4)}_{16}$ obtained in a similar way to the previously defined $C_{R(3,3)}$ by respectively taking the two Ramsey $3$-coloring of a complete graph on $16$ vertices that avoid monochromatic triangles~\cite{greenwood1955combinatorial, kalbfleisch1968maximal, laywine1988simple, radziszowski2011small} and coloring the vertices with the fourth color.

nodes.name: Extremal four-color family G^(4)_ex
nodes.statement:
Mirroring the construction of $\mathcal{G}^{(3)}_\textrm{ex}$, we let $\mathcal{G}^{(4)}_\textrm{ex} \subset \mathcal{G}^{(4)}$ consist of all colorings that can be obtained by

\begin{itemize} \setlength\itemsep{0em}
    \item[(i)] selecting an element in $\mathcal{B}_\mathbf{1/16} (C'_{R(3,3,3)} )$ or $\mathcal{B}_\mathbf{1/16} (C''_{R(3,3,3)} )$,
    \item[(ii)] recoloring some of the edges from any of the first, second or third color to instead use the fourth color without creating any additional monochromatic triangles,
    \item[(iii)] applying any permutation of the four colors.
nodes.statement_short: Colorings from balanced blow-ups of $C'$ or $C''$, recolored into the fourth color without new triangles, up to color permutation.

nodes.name: Four-color triangle stability theorem
nodes.statement: There exists an $n_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for any $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that any $G \in \mathcal{G}_n^{(4)}$ of order $n \geq n_0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^cp(K_3^i; G) \leq m_4(3; n) + \delta$ can be turned into an element of $\mathcal{G}^{(4)}_\textrm{ex}$ by recoloring at most $\varepsilon \binom{n}{2}$ edges.
nodes.statement_short: Near-optimal 4-colorings of $K_n$ are $\varepsilon\binom n2$-close to $\mathcal{G}^{(4)}_\textrm{ex}$.
assumptions: $G \in \mathcal{G}_n^{(4)}$ of order $n \geq n_0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^cp(K_3^i; G) \leq m_4(3; n) + \delta$
conclusions: can be turned into an element of $\mathcal{G}^{(4)}_\textrm{ex}$ by recoloring at most $\varepsilon \binom{n}{2}$ edges
nodes.label: eq:fourcolortriangles

nodes.name: Extremal four-colorings lie in G^(4)_ex
nodes.statement: Note that this implies that any large enough element in $\mathcal{G}_n^{(4)}$ minimizing the number of monochromatic triangles must be in $\mathcal{G}^{(4)}_\textrm{ex}$.
assumptions: any large enough element in $\mathcal{G}_n^{(4)}$ minimizing the number of monochromatic triangles

nodes.name: Off-diagonal Ramsey multiplicity m(t_1,...,t_c;n)
Symmetric off-diagonal Ramsey multiplicity m_s
Limits m(t_1,...,t_c) and m_s(t_1,...,t_c)
nodes.statement: We will use $m(t_1, \ldots, t_c)$ as well as $m_s(t_1, \ldots, t_c)$ to respectively denote the limits of both of these functions as $n$ tends to infinity.

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Proposition 2.4
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound from the off-diagonal Ramsey blow-up bound with $R(3,3)=6$; lower bound via the improved flag algebra calculus.

nodes.name: Off-diagonal Ramsey upper bound (2.4)
nodes.statement: m(t_1, \ldots, t_c) \leq (R(t_1, \ldots, t_{c-1}) - 1)^{1-t_c}
nodes.label: eq:ramsey_upper_offdiag

nodes.name: Flag
nodes.statement: A \emph{flag} $F = (G, \psi)$ consists of a coloring $G \in \mathcal{G}^{(c)}$ along with a partial but distinct labeling of its vertex set  $\psi: [k] \hookrightarrow V(G)$ for some non-negative integer $k$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Isomorphic flags
nodes.statement: Two flags $F = (G, \psi)$ and $F' = (G', \psi')$ are \emph{isomorphic}, denoted by $F \simeq F'$, if there exists a bijection $\varphi: V(G) \overset{\sim}{\hookrightarrow} V(G')$ such that $G \equiv G' \circ \varphi$ and $\psi' \equiv \varphi \circ \psi$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Type
nodes.statement: If $k = v(G)$ on the other hand, we refer to $F$ as a \emph{type} and will commonly use the notation $\tau$ for it.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Empty type
nodes.statement: When $k = v(G) = 0$, we refer to it as the \emph{empty type} $\varnothing$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Subflag
nodes.statement: Given some flag $F = (G, \psi)$ and subset of its vertices $\operatorname{im} (\psi) \subseteq S \subseteq V(G)$, we write $F[S] = (G[S], \psi)$ and say $F[S]$ is  a \emph{subflag} of $F$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Flag of type tau
nodes.statement: We say that $F$ is \emph{of type $\tau$} if its labeled part is isomorphic to $\tau$, that is if $F[\operatorname{im} (\psi)] \simeq \tau$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Flag families F^tau
nodes.statement: We denote the set of arbitrary but canonical representatives of isomorphism classes of flags of a given type $\tau$ by $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ and we use $\mathcal{F}^\tau_n$ to refer to those of order $n$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Tuple density
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities
nodes.statement_short: Fraction of sunflowers of labelled vertex sets in $F$ that induce copies of $F_1,\ldots,F_\ell$.

nodes.name: Density and pair density of flags
nodes.statement: We will in fact only need the cases where $\ell = 1$ (the \emph{density}) and $\ell = 2$ (the \emph{pair density}) and note that for $\tau = \varnothing$ the notion of density aligns with the density of colorings defined in the previous section, that is we have $p(H; G) = p\big((H, \varnothing); (G, \varnothing) \big)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities

nodes.name: Averaging (chain rule) for flag densities
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities
nodes.statement_short: Tuple densities in $F$ average over intermediate flags $F'$ of order $k$.
assumptions: a given type $\tau$, flags $F_1, \ldots, F_\ell, F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$ and integer $k$ satisfying $v(F_1) + \ldots + v(F_\ell) - (\ell-1) \, v(\tau) \leq k \leq v(F)$
nodes.label: lemma:double_counting

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement:
For each $S \in\mathbf S(F'; F)$ let $\iota_S: V(F') \overset{\sim}{\hookrightarrow} S \subseteq V(G)$ be an arbitrary but fixed bijection.
        There is a natural map $\mathbf{S}(F_1,\dots,F_\ell; F') \times \mathbf{S}(F'; F) \to \mathbf{S}(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F)$ given by mapping $(S_1,\dots,S_\ell)\in \mathbf S(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F')$ and $S \in \mathbf{S}(F'; F)$ to $(\iota_S(S_1),\dots,\iota_S(S_\ell))$. This map is surjective and the pre-image of every point is of equal cardinality.
        
        Since any $(S_1,\dots, S_\ell)\in\mathbf S(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F)$ satisfies $F[S_i]\simeq F_i$  for all $1\le i\le \ell$ if and only if all elements $(S_1',\dots,S_\ell)'\in \mathbf S(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F')$ and $S \in \mathbf{S}(F'; F)$ in its pre-image also satisfy $F[S] \simeq F'$ as well as $F'[S_i']\simeq F_i$ for all $1\le i\le \ell$,  the desired statement follows.
nodes.section: 3.1 Flags and types, and their densities
nodes.statement_short: Double counting via a surjective map between sunflower families with equal-size fibres.

nodes.name: Kernel K^tau
nodes.statement:
For a given type $\tau$, we consider elements in $\mathbb{R} \mathcal{F}^\tau$, that is arbitrary finite linear combinations of elements in $\mathcal{F}^\tau$, and let

\begin{equation} \mathcal{K}^\tau = \operatorname{span} \left\{ F'  - \sum_{F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau_{ n}} p(F';F) \, F  \mid F' \in \mathcal{F}^\tau, \, n \geq v(F') \right\} \subset \mathbb{R} \mathcal{F}^\tau
\end{equation}

denote the subspace of $\mathbb{R} \mathcal{F}^\tau$ spanned by the kernel of the density equalities given by \cref{lemma:double_counting}.

nodes.name: Kernel of density equalities (3.1)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{K}^\tau = \operatorname{span} \left\{ F'  - \sum_{F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau_{ n}} p(F';F) \, F  \mid F' \in \mathcal{F}^\tau, \, n \geq v(F') \right\} \subset \mathbb{R} \mathcal{F}^\tau
nodes.label: eq:definition_of_kernel

nodes.name: Flag algebra
nodes.statement: The \emph{flag algebra $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ of type $\tau$} is given by furnishing the quotient space $\mathbb R\mathcal{F}^\tau / \mathcal{K}^\tau$ with a product through the bilinear extension of $F \cdot F' = \sum_{G \in \mathcal{F}^\tau_{ n}} p(F, F'; G) \cdot G$, defined for any $F, F' \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$ and $n = v(F) + v(F') - v(\tau)$.
nodes.statement_short: Quotient $\mathbb R\mathcal F^\tau/\mathcal K^\tau$ with product given by pair densities.
nodes.label: def:flagalgebra

nodes.name: Flag product is well defined
nodes.statement: Note that by \cref{lemma:double_counting}, the bilinear extension in the definition of the product is well defined and in fact independent of $n$ as long as $n \geq v(F) + v(F') - v(\tau)$.

nodes.name: Density of algebra elements
nodes.statement: We can also extend our notion of density so that the expression $p(f_1,\dots,f_\ell;F)$ is well-defined as along as $f_1, \ldots, f_\ell$ can be expressed in $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ as the sum of cosets corresponding to flags of order at most $v(F)$.

nodes.name: Identification of flags with cosets
nodes.statement: We identify flags $F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$ with their coset $F + \mathcal{K}^\tau$ in $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ for notational convenience, i.e., we treat $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ as a subset of $\mathcal{A}^\tau$, and whenever an element from $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ does not necessarily correspond to (the coset of) a flag, we will use lower case letters to denote it.

nodes.name: Expansion of algebra elements in flags
nodes.statement_short: Every algebra element equals $\sum_F p(f;F)F$ over flags of any large enough order $n$.

nodes.name: Convergent sequence of flags
nodes.statement: Let $(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of flags in $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ of increasing order and assume that $\lim_{n \to \infty} p(F; F_n)$ exists for any $F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$. We call such a sequence \emph{convergent} and note that by compactness any sequence of flags of increasing order contains a convergent subsequence.

nodes.name: Positive homomorphisms
nodes.statement: On the other side, let $\operatorname{Hom}^+(\mathcal{A}^\tau, \mathbb{R}) = \{\phi \in \operatorname{Hom} (\mathcal{A}^\tau, \mathbb{R}) \mid \phi(F) \geq 0 \text{ for all } F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau \}$ denote the set of \emph{positive homomorphisms}, that is all real algebra homomorphisms mapping the cosets corresponding to flags in $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ to positive values.

nodes.name: Correspondence of positive homomorphisms and convergent sequences
nodes.statement: Let a type $\tau$ be given. For any $\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}^+(\mathcal{A}^\tau, \mathbb{R})$ there exists a convergent sequence $(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ satisfying $\lim_{n \to \infty} p(f; F_n) = \phi(f)$ for all $f \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$ and vice-versa.
nodes.statement_short: Positive homomorphisms are exactly limits of convergent flag sequences.
equivalent_conditions: a convergent sequence $(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ satisfying $\lim_{n \to \infty} p(f; F_n) = \phi(f)$ for all $f \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$
nodes.label: thm:homfunctional

nodes.name: Semantic cone
nodes.statement: This means the goal becomes to identify elements in the \emph{semantic cone} $\mathcal{S}^\tau = \{f \in \mathcal{A}^\tau \mid \phi(f) \geq 0 \text{ for all } \phi \in \operatorname{Hom}^+(\mathcal{A}^\tau, \mathbb{R})\}$, as these correspond to combinatorial relations that are {\lq}true{\rq} for any sequence.

nodes.name: Partial order on A^tau
nodes.statement: For notational convenience, we will let $\mathcal{S}^\tau$ define a partial order on $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ by saying that $f \geq g$ for $f, g \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$ if and only if $f - g \in \mathcal{S}^\tau$.

nodes.name: Positivity formulation of the four-color problem
nodes.statement_short: The four-color result amounts to $f_0=\sum_i K_3^i-1/256$ lying in the semantic cone.

nodes.name: Tight positive element and extremal homomorphism
nodes.statement: Finally, we say that a positive element $f_0 \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$ is \emph{tight} if there exists a positive homomorphism that is \emph{extremal} for $f_0$, that is some $\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}^+(\mathcal{A}^\tau, \mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfying $\phi(f_0) = 0$.

nodes.name: Tightness via extremal sequences
nodes.statement: By \cref{thm:homfunctional} this is of course equivalent to requiring the existance of a convergent sequence in $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ that is \emph{extremal} for $f_0$, that is some $(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfying $\lim_{n \to \infty} p(f_0; F_n) = 0$.

nodes.name: Downward operator
nodes.statement_short: Unlabel a $\tau$-flag and weight it by the probability $q_\tau(F)$ that a random labelling reproduces it; extend linearly.
nodes.label: def:downward

nodes.name: Downward operator is order-preserving
nodes.statement: If $f \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$ is a positive element, then its image $\llbracket f \rrbracket_{\tau}$ in $\mathcal{A}^\varnothing$ is as well.
conclusions: its image $\llbracket f \rrbracket_{\tau}$ in $\mathcal{A}^\varnothing$ is as well
nodes.label: lemma:orderpreserving

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement:
For each $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an integer $n_0 = n_0(f, \varepsilon)$ such that $f$ can be expressed as a linear combination of elements in $\mathcal{F}^\tau_{n}$ while also satisfying
    $p(f,F)\ge -\varepsilon$ and therefore $p(f+\varepsilon,F)\ge 0$ for  any $F\in \mathcal{F}^\tau_{n}$ with $n \geq n_0$. 
    Otherwise, there would exist a positive homomorphism $\phi$ by \cref{thm:homfunctional} satisfying $\phi(f)<-\varepsilon$, contradicting the assumption that $f$ is a positive element. We now have
    \[
    \llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau+\varepsilon \cdot q_{\tau}(\tau)
    \ge
    \llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau +\varepsilon \cdot q_{\tau}(\tau) \cdot \tau\vert_\tau 
    =
    \llbracket f+\varepsilon \rrbracket_\tau
    =
    \sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}^\tau_{n}} p(f+\varepsilon,F) \, \llbracket F\rrbracket_\tau
    \ge 0,
    \]
    where in the first and last step we have used that $0 = 0 \cdot \varnothing \leq \tau\vert_\tau  \leq 1 \cdot \varnothing = 1$, which is in fact true for any flag in $\mathcal{F}^\varnothing$, and then for the second and third step, respectively, the linearity of the downward operator and the fact that f, and therefore also $f + \varepsilon$, is expressible as a linear combination of elements in $\mathcal{F}_{n}^\tau$. Since $q_\tau(\tau)$ is a constant, it follows that $\llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau \geq -\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and hence $\llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau \geq 0$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $f$ by nonnegative flag combinations up to $\varepsilon$ using Theorem 3.3, push down linearly, and let $\varepsilon\to0$.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for flag algebras
nodes.statement: For any type $\tau$ and $f \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$, we have $\llbracket f^2 \rrbracket_\tau \geq \llbracket f \rrbracket_\tau^2$.
nodes.label: lemma:cauchyschwarz

nodes.name: Sum-of-squares lower bound (3.2)
nodes.statement: f_0 \geq \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \sum_{g \in \mathcal{B}^\tau} \llbracket g^2 \rrbracket_\tau
nodes.label: eq:basic-sos

nodes.name: SOS certificate equation (3.3)
nodes.statement: f_0 = \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \sum_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{F}^\tau_{ \ell_\tau }|} \left\llbracket \left( \sum_{F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau_{ \ell_\tau }} c^\tau_{i, F} \cdot F \right)^2 \right\rrbracket_\tau + \sum_{F \in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing_N} s_F \cdot F
nodes.label: eq:sos_certificate

nodes.name: SOS certificate and slack
Sharp flag
nodes.statement: We say a flag $F \in \mathcal{F}_N^\varnothing$ is \emph{sharp} in a given certificate if $s_F = 0$.

nodes.name: Non-sharp flags vanish in extremal homomorphisms
nodes.statement: If a flag $F \in \mathcal{F}_N^\varnothing$ is not sharp in a given certificate of the positivity of some tight $f_0$, then $\phi (F) = 0$ for any $\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}^+(\mathcal{A}^\varnothing, \mathbb{R}^n)$ that is extremal for $f_0$.
assumptions: a flag $F \in \mathcal{F}_N^\varnothing$ is not sharp in a given certificate of the positivity of some tight $f_0$
conclusions: $\phi (F) = 0$ for any $\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}^+(\mathcal{A}^\varnothing, \mathbb{R}^n)$ that is extremal for $f_0$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.8
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the certificate at an extremal homomorphism: all terms are nonnegative and sum to zero.

nodes.name: Goodman's SOS certificate
nodes.label: ex:Goodman_SOS

nodes.name: Data matrices
Data matrix definition
nodes.statement: D_F^\tau = \left( p \big( \left\llbracket F_1 \cdot F_2 \right\rrbracket_\tau; F \big) \right) \in \mathbb{Q}^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau} \times \mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}}
nodes.label: eq:density_matrix

nodes.name: SOS certificates correspond to SDP solutions
nodes.statement_short: The SOS coefficients form a certificate iff the Gram matrices $Q^\tau=(C^\tau)^\top C^\tau$ satisfy the linear SDP constraints (3.4).

nodes.name: SDP certificate equation (3.4)
nodes.statement: p(f_0;F)  = \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \left\langle Q^\tau, D_F^\tau \right\rangle + s_F,
nodes.label: eq:sdp_certificate

nodes.name: SDP certificate
Blocks
nodes.statement: Let us remark that we will refer to $Q^\tau$ and $D_F^\tau$ as \emph{blocks}, since in the context of semidefinite programming one would consider them part of larger block-diagonal matrices $Q \succeq 0$ and $D_F$, so that \cref{eq:sdp_certificate} simply becomes $p(f;F)  = \left\langle Q, D_F \right\rangle + s_F$ for all $F \in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing_N$.

nodes.name: SDP formulation of Goodman's problem
nodes.statement_short: Data matrices of Goodman's problem with $N=3$ and the PSD matrix $Q$ completing the certificate.
nodes.label: ex:Goodman_SDP

nodes.name: Flags avoiding H
nodes.statement: For this, we denote by $\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\mathcal{H}} = \{ F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau \mid p(H; F)=0 \}$ the collection of all flags $F$ satisfying not containing any $H\in\mathcal{H}$.

nodes.name: Algebra A_H with forbidden subflags
nodes.statement: This defines an algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}$ as before.

nodes.name: Color and type-index permutation pair
nodes.statement: To be more precise, let $\tau$ be a given type and $(\alpha, \beta)$ a pair consisting of a color permutation $\alpha: [c] \overset{\sim}{\hookrightarrow} [c]$ and a permutation of the type indices $\beta: [v(\tau)] \overset{\sim}{\hookrightarrow} [v(\tau)]$.

nodes.name: Permuted flag pi^{alpha,beta}(F)
nodes.statement: For every $\tau$-flag $F = (G, \psi)$, we now denote by $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F) = (\alpha \circ F, \psi \circ \beta)$ the flag obtained by permuting the colors and type indices according to $(\alpha, \beta)$.

nodes.name: pi^{alpha,beta} is a bijection of flag families
nodes.statement: Note that the flag $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)$ is of type $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)$, so that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}$ defines a bijection from $\mathcal{F}^\tau$ to $\mathcal{F}^{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}$.

nodes.name: Color/vertex permutations induce algebra isomorphisms
nodes.statement:
The linear extension of $\pi^{\alpha, \beta}$ induces an algebra homomorphism from $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ to $\mathcal{A}^{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}$ that satisfies
    
    \begin{equation} \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_1 \cdot f_2) = \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_1) \cdot \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_2)
    \end{equation}
    
    for any $f_1, f_2 \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$ as well as
    
    \begin{equation} p \big( \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_1), \ldots, \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_\ell); \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(F) \big) = p(f_1, \ldots, f_\ell; F).
    \end{equation}
    
    for any $f_1, \ldots, f_\ell \in \mathcal{A}^\tau$ and $F \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}$ extends to an algebra homomorphism preserving products and densities.
conclusions: The linear extension of $\pi^{\alpha, \beta}$ induces an algebra homomorphism from $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ to $\mathcal{A}^{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}$
nodes.label: lemma:extend_color_vertex_permutations

nodes.name: Permutation commutes with product (4.1)
nodes.statement: \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_1 \cdot f_2) = \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_1) \cdot \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_2)
nodes.label: eq:product_commute

nodes.name: Permutation preserves density (4.2)
nodes.statement: p \big( \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_1), \ldots, \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(f_\ell); \pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(F) \big) = p(f_1, \ldots, f_\ell; F).
nodes.label: eq:density_permutation

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement:
We start by noting that \cref{eq:density_permutation} holds for \emph{flags} $F_1, \ldots, F_\ell \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$,
    
    since for any $i\in \{1,\dots,\ell\}$ and $(S_1, \ldots, S_\ell) \in {\bf S}(F_1, \ldots, F_\ell; F)$ we have $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)\vert_{S_i} \simeq \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_i)$ if and only if $F\vert_{S_i} \simeq F_i$. 
    
    Using this, it immediately follows that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\mathcal{K}^\tau) \subseteq \mathcal{K}^{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}$ and that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}$ likewise commutes with the multiplication of flags, since for $F_1, F_2\in\mathcal{F}^\tau$ we have
    
    \begin{align*}
        \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1\cdot F_2) & = \sum_{H\in\mathcal{F}_n^\tau} p(F_1,F_2;H) \, \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(H) \\
        & = \sum_{H\in\mathcal{F}_n^\tau} p(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1),\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_2);\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(H)) \, \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(H) \\
        & = \sum_{H \in \mathcal{F}_n^{\pi^{\alpha, \beta}(\tau)}}  p(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1),\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_2);H) \, H \\
        & = \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1)\cdot\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_2)
    \end{align*}
    
    for some large enough $n$. It follows that the linear extension of $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}$ induces an algebra homomorphism from $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ to $\mathcal{A}^{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}$ and that \cref{eq:product_commute} as well as \cref{eq:density_permutation} hold for arbitrary algebra elements by linearity.
nodes.statement_short: Check density invariance on flags, deduce kernel and product compatibility, extend by linearity.

nodes.name: Permutations commute with the downward operator
nodes.statement: We have $\llbracket \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(f) \rrbracket_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} = \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}(\llbracket f \rrbracket_{\tau})$ for any $f \in\mathcal{F}^\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Downward operator commutes with color/type permutations.
nodes.label: lemma:harmonic_downward

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement:
Let us first show that the statement is true for any flag $F = (G,\psi) \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$. We note that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)\vert_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} = (\alpha\circ G,\varnothing) = \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}(F\vert_\tau)$. For the coefficient, we likewise have
    
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        q_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F))
        &=&
        \frac{|\{\varphi : [v(\tau)] \hookrightarrow V(G) \mid (\alpha\circ G, \varphi\circ \beta) \simeq (\alpha\circ G,\psi\circ \beta) \}|}{v(G)! \, / \, (v(G)-v(\tau))!},
    \end{eqnarray*}
    
    since $(\alpha\circ G,\varphi\circ \beta) \simeq (\alpha\circ G,\psi\circ \beta)$ if and only if $(G,\varphi) \simeq F$.
    
    It follows that 
    
    \begin{align*}
        \llbracket \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F) \rrbracket_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} & = q_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)) \cdot \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)\vert_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} \\
        
        
        
        & = q_\tau(F) \cdot \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}( F \vert_\tau )
        
        = \pi^{\alpha, \varnothing}\big( q_\tau(F) \cdot F \vert_\tau \big) \\
        
        & = \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}(\llbracket F \rrbracket_{\tau}).
    \end{align*}
    
    The statement now follows for all elements in $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ by linearity.
nodes.statement_short: Verify on flags by comparing unlabelled flags and the coefficients $q_\tau$, then extend by linearity.

nodes.name: Admissible color permutations and generalized isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Color permutations fixing $f_0$, flag equivalence up to them and type-index permutations, canonical representatives, and generalized automorphism groups.

nodes.name: Admissible permutations for the four-color triangle problem
nodes.statement: In the case of $f_0 = K_3^1 + K_3^2 + K_3^3 + K_3^4 - 1/256$, we have $\Upsilon = S_{[4]}$.

nodes.name: Upsilon-averaged data matrices
Reindexed matrix M^{(alpha,beta)}
Data matrices transform equivariantly
nodes.statement_short: Reindexing data matrices by $(\alpha,\beta)$ equals the data matrix of the permuted type and flag; averaged ones are invariant.
nodes.label: lem:averaged_are_invariant

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.5
nodes.statement:
Let $F_1, F_2 \in \mathcal{F}^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)}_N$. For the first equality, we have
    
    \begin{align*}
        (D_F^\tau)^{(\alpha, \beta)}_{F_1,F_2} &=
        (D_F^\tau)_{\pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_1), \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_2)} \\
        & = p \left( \big\llbracket \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_1) \cdot \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})}(F_2) \big\rrbracket_{\tau} ; F \right) \\
        & = p \left( \pi^{(\alpha, \varnothing)} \left( \big\llbracket \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_1 \cdot F_2) \big\rrbracket_{\tau} \right); \pi^{(\alpha, \varnothing)} (F) \right) \\
        & = p(\left\llbracket F_1 \cdot F_2 \right\rrbracket_{\pi^{(\alpha, \beta)}(\tau)}; \pi^{(\alpha, \varnothing)} (F)) \\
        & = \big( D_{\pi^{(\alpha,\varnothing)}(F)}^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)} \big)_{F_1,F_2}.
    \end{align*}
    
    For the second equality, we have
    
    \begin{align*}
        (\hat D^\tau_{F})^{(\alpha,\beta)}_{F_1,F_2} 
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} \left( D^\tau_{\pi^{(\alpha',\varnothing)} (F)} \right)^{(\alpha, \beta)}_{F_1, F_2} \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} p(\llbracket \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})}(F_1 \cdot F_2) \rrbracket_\tau; \pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)) \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon}  p(\pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \varnothing)} (\llbracket (F_1 \cdot F_2) \rrbracket_{\pi^{(\alpha, \beta)} (\tau)} ); \pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)) \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} p(\left\llbracket F_1 \cdot F_2 \right\rrbracket_{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)}; \pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)) \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} \left( D^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)}_{\pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)} \right)_{F_1, F_2} \\
        & = \big( \hat D_F^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)} \big)_{F_1, F_2}.
    \end{align*}
    
    Here we have made use of \cref{lemma:extend_color_vertex_permutations} as well as \cref{lemma:harmonic_downward} for both arguments.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.7
nodes.statement:
By assumption, for all  $F \in \mathcal{F}_n^\varnothing$
     \begin{equation*}
         p(f_0; F) = \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}}\left\langle Q^{\tau},   D_{F }^{\tau } \right\rangle + s_{ F }.
    \end{equation*}
    
    Then, in particular
    
     \begin{align*}
          \sum_{\alpha \in \Upsilon} p(f_0; \pi^{(\alpha,\varnothing)} (F)) 
          &= \sum_{\alpha \in \Upsilon} \left(\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}}\left\langle Q^{\tau},   D_{\pi^{(\alpha,\varnothing)} (F) }^{\tau } \right\rangle + s_{ \pi^{(\alpha,\varnothing)} (F) } \right) \\
        |\Upsilon| p(f_0; F) &= \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}}\left\langle Q^{\tau}, \sum_{\alpha \in \Upsilon}  D_{\pi^{(\alpha,\varnothing)} (F) }^{\tau } \right\rangle + \sum_{\alpha \in \Upsilon} s_{ \pi^{(\alpha,\varnothing)} (F) } \\
        p(f_0; F) &= \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}}\left\langle Q^{\tau}, \hat{D}_{F }^{\tau } \right\rangle + \hat{s}_{ F } \\
        &= \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}}\left\langle Q^{\eta(\tau)}, (\hat{D}_{F }^{\tau})^{\eta(\tau)} \right\rangle + \hat{s}_{ F } \\
        &= \sum_{\sigma\in \mu(\mathcal{T})}\left\langle 
        \sum_{\substack{\tau \in \mathcal{T} \\ \mu(\tau) = \sigma}} (Q^\tau)^{\eta(\tau)}, \hat{D}_{F }^{\sigma} \right\rangle + \hat{s}_{ F },
    \end{align*}
    
    establishing the claim.

nodes.name: Theoretical optimal block-diagonalization
nodes.statement:
Let $R$ denote the $\mathbb R$-subalgebra of the matrix ring $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}})$ that is generated by all matrices $\hat D^\tau_F$ as $F$ varies in $\mu(\mathcal{F})$. Since $R$ is generated by symmetric matrices, it follows that the vector space $\mathbb R^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}}$ is a semi-simple $R$-module. Indeed, the orthogonal complement of any $R$-invariant subspace is again $R$-invariant. By \cite[pp. 654, Proposition 4.7]{SergeLang2002}, $R$ is semi-simple, so $R = \prod_{j\in J} R_j$ with each $R_j$ a simple ring.

We can find in $\mathbb R^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}}$ a simple $R_j$-subspace for every $j\in J$. This is because the unit $e_j$ of $R_j$ is non-zero in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}})$ and so $R_j$ acts faithfully on $\mathbb R^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}}$. Such a subspace $V_j$ may be found in the isotypic subspace $e_j\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}}$. By Wedderburn's Theorem \cite[pp. 649, Corollary 3.5]{SergeLang2002}:

\[
    R_j \simeq \operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(R_j)}(V_j)
\]

and by Frobenius's theorem we know that $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{R}}(R_j)\in \{\mathbb R,\mathbb C, \mathbb H\}$.
In other words, there exists a unique sequence $(n_j,K_j)\in \mathbb N\times \{\mathbb R, \mathbb C, \mathbb H\}$ so that
\begin{equation} R_j \simeq \operatorname{Mat}^{n_j\times n_j}(K_j)
    \quad \text{ and }
    \quad 
    R \simeq \bigoplus_{j\in J} \operatorname{Mat}^{n_j\times n_j}(K_j).
\end{equation}
The matrices $B^\tau$ that we are looking for, are those base change matrices that witness the second isomorphism in \cref{eq:ring_minimal_decomposition}.
nodes.statement_short: The algebra generated by the data matrices is semisimple; by Wedderburn and Frobenius it is a sum of matrix algebras over R, C or H.

nodes.name: Rational isotypic decomposition
nodes.statement: We therefore derived our own, simplified partial block-diagonalization, that we will refer to as a \emph{rational isotypic decomposition}, in order to provide an efficient diagonalization involving rational base change matrices only.

nodes.name: Isotypic units from irreducible characters
nodes.statement:
Letting $R = \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R[\Lambda_\tau]}(\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{F}^{\tau}_{\ell_\tau}})$, there is a bijection between the simple rings $R_j$ and the irreducible characters $\chi$ of $\Lambda_\tau$. Given an irreducible character $\chi$,
    the unit $e_\chi$ of the simple ring $R_\chi$ is
    \[
        e_\chi = \frac{\operatorname{deg}(\chi)}{|\Lambda_\tau|}\sum_{g\in \Lambda_\tau} \chi(g^{-1}) g.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Simple components of the commutant correspond to irreducible characters, with central idempotents $e_\chi$.

nodes.name: Isotypic components for Goodman's problem
Rational Isotypic Decomposition
nodes.statement:
\caption{Rational Isotypic Decomposition} \begin{algorithmic}[2]
        \REQUIRE A group $\Lambda_\tau$, an action $\Lambda_\tau\times [\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}]\to [\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}]$
        \ENSURE Every $V_\chi$ has a rational basis and $\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}} = \bigoplus_{\chi\in C\cup\{\chi^\bot\}} V_\chi$
        \STATE $ C \gets \varnothing$
        \STATE $ \chi^\bot \gets (0,\dots,0) $
        \FOR{$\chi$ an irreducible character of $\Lambda_\tau$}
            \IF{ $\chi$ is rational}
                \STATE $C \gets C \cup \{\chi\}$
            \ELSIF{$\chi+\overline{\chi}$ is rational}
                \STATE $C \gets C \cup \{\chi+\overline{\chi}\}$
            \ELSE
                \STATE $\chi^\bot = \chi^\bot + \chi$
            \ENDIF
        \ENDFOR
        \FOR{$\chi$ in $C\cup \{\chi^\bot\}$}
            \STATE $V_\chi \gets \operatorname{im}(\frac{\operatorname{deg}(\chi)}{|\Lambda_\tau|}\sum_{g\in \Lambda_\tau} \chi(g^{-1}) g)$ 
        \ENDFOR
        \RETURN $\{V_\chi\}$
    \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Group irreducible characters into rational classes and project onto isotypic components to get rational invariant subspaces.
output: Every $V_\chi$ has a rational basis and $\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{F}^\tau_{\ell_\tau}} = \bigoplus_{\chi\in C\cup\{\chi^\bot\}} V_\chi$
nodes.label: alg:Rational_Isotypic

nodes.name: Relation to Razborov's invariant-anti-invariant split
nodes.statement: Finally, let us note that Razborov proposed an invariant-anti-invariant-split in \cite{Razborov_2010}. This can also be considered within the framework of block diagonalization, by viewing it as a further simplification of our rational isotypic decomposition. In Razborov's case, one only computes the isotypic component of $\chi = \chi_{\operatorname{triv}}$, which is called the invariant part, where $\chi_{\operatorname{triv}} = (1,\dots, 1)$ is the trivial character. Afterwards, we take the complement of the invariant space $V_{\chi_{\operatorname{triv}}}$, which is called the anti-invariant part. Our method results in a more significant reduction in the number of variables, while still being relatively easy to implement and taking a reasonable amount of compute power to run even for larger problems.

They will satisfy
\[
    0 < \frac{1}{n_0} < \varepsilon_0 < \frac{1}{n_1} < \varepsilon_1 <
    \varepsilon_2 < \varepsilon_3 < \frac{1}{n_2} < \varepsilon_4
    < \varepsilon_5 < \varepsilon_6 < \varepsilon_7 <
    1-\delta_0 < \varepsilon_8 < 1
\]
along with certain constraints that are not further specified here but will be \whiteboxedchar{highlighted} throughout for emphasis.

nodes.name: Standard and alpha-standard flags
nodes.statement: A flag $F\in\mathcal{F}^\varnothing$ is \emph{standard} if $p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; F)= 0$. It is \emph{$\alpha$-standard} for some $\alpha>0$ if additionally  $p(\hat K_3;F) \le  \alpha$.

nodes.name: Random subsets are standard with high probability
nodes.statement:
Assume \boxedchar{A1}, \boxedchar{A2}, and \boxedchar{A3}. For a subset of $\mathscr M \subseteq V(G)$ of size $n_1$ chosen uniformly at random, we have 
\[
    \mathbb P[G[\mathscr M] \text{ is }
    (\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)\text{-standard}]
    \ge 1 - 
    \left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon_1(1+\varepsilon_1)} + \frac{\binom{n_1}{6}}{s} \right)
    \left(p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma\right)
    -
    \left( 
    \frac{1}{1+\varepsilon_1}+\frac{1}{s}
    \right)
    \varepsilon_1.
\]
nodes.section: 5.2 Definition and existence of standard flags
nodes.statement_short: A random $n_1$-subset of $G$ is $(\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)$-standard with probability close to 1 when $p(\hat K_3;G)$ is near $\varsigma$.
assumptions: a subset of $\mathscr M \subseteq V(G)$ of size $n_1$ chosen uniformly at random
nodes.label: lem:Claim_1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lemma:double_counting}, we have both
    
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb E[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M])]
        =
        p(\hat K_3;G) \quad \text{and} \quad
        \mathbb E[p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3};G[\mathscr M])]
        =
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3};G).
    \end{align*}
    
    Let $x=\mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M])>\varsigma+\varepsilon_1]$ and note that, for \whiteboxedchar{sufficiently large $n_0$}, we have by \boxedchar{A1} that $p(\hat K_3; G)\ge \varsigma-\varepsilon_1^2$.
    By approximating $p(\hat K_3;G)$ through a step function, we have
    \[
    (\varsigma-\varepsilon_1^2) \, (1-x)
    +
    (\varsigma+\varepsilon_1) \, x  
    \le
    p(\hat K_3;G),
    \]
    and therefore
    
    \begin{equation} \mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M] > \varsigma + \varepsilon_1) = x
        \le
        \frac{p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma+\varepsilon_1^2}{\varepsilon_1(1+\varepsilon_1)}.
    \end{equation}
    
    Using Markov's inequality, we get
    
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P[ 
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; G[\mathscr M]) > 0] &\leq \mathbb P \left[p(\hat K_{3,1};G[\mathscr M]) \ge \binom{n_1}{4}^{-1} \right]
        +\mathbb P \left[p(\hat K_{3,3};G[\mathscr M]) \ge \binom{n_1}{6}^{-1} \right] \\ 
        &\le \binom{n_1}{4} \, p(\hat K_{3,1};G)
        +\binom{n_1}{6} \, p(\hat K_{3,3};G).
    \end{align*}
    
    Using \boxedchar{A2}, we have for \whiteboxedchar{sufficiently large $n_0$}
    \[
        p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma
        \ge
        s\left(p(\hat K_{3,1};G) + p(\hat K_{3,3}; G)\right) - \varepsilon_1 \binom{n_1}{6}^{-1}.
    \]
    
    Assuming that \whiteboxedchar{$n_1$ is large enough} for ${n_1 \choose 4} \leq {n_1 \choose 6}$ to hold, we therefore get
    
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb P[ 
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; G[\mathscr M]) > 0] \le \frac{\binom{n_1}{6}(p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma)+\varepsilon_1}{s}. \end{equation}
    
    Finally, through the union bound and by combining \cref{eq:k3bnd} as well as \cref{eq:k31k33bnd}, we therefore get
    
    \begin{align*}
        & \quad \mathbb P[G[\mathscr M] \text{ is } (\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)\text{-standard}] \\
        & = 1 - \mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M]) >  \varsigma+\varepsilon_1 \vee 
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; G[\mathscr M]) > 0] \\
        & \geq 1 - \mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M]) >  \varsigma+\varepsilon_1] - \mathbb P[ 
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; G[\mathscr M]) > 0] \\
        & \geq 1 - \frac{p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma+\varepsilon_1^2}{\varepsilon_1(1+\varepsilon_1)} - \frac{\binom{n_1}{6}(p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma)+\varepsilon_1}{s} \\
        & = 1 - 
            \left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon_1(1+\varepsilon_1)} + \frac{\binom{n_1}{6}}{s} \right)
            \left(p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma\right)
            -
            \left( 
            \frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon_1}+\frac{1}{s}
            \right)
            \varepsilon_1,
    \end{align*}
    
    implying the statement of the lemma.

nodes.statement_short: Bound the two failure events separately (step function averaging and Markov's inequality with A2) and take a union bound.

nodes.name: Edges from a vertex to a maximal clique
nodes.statement:
Let $F$ be standard. Let $X \in \mathcal{X}_F$ and $c_1$ the color of the monochromatic clique $F[X]$. For any
$y \in V(F)\setminus X$
there exists at most one edge $e_0 \in y \ast X$ with $F(e_0) = c_1$ as well as a color $c_2 \neq c_1$ such that $F(e) = c_2$ for all $e \in y \ast X \setminus \{e_0\}$.
assumptions: $X \in \mathcal{X}_F$ and $c_1$ the color of the monochromatic clique $F[X]$
conclusions: there exists at most one edge $e_0 \in y \ast X$ with $F(e_0) = c_1$ as well as a color $c_2 \neq c_1$ such that $F(e) = c_2$ for all $e \in y \ast X \setminus \{e_0\}$
nodes.label: lem:Claim_2

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5.5
nodes.statement:
If there exists an edge $e_0 \in y \ast X$ satisfying $F(e_0) = c_1$, then all other edges in $y \ast X$ must be monochromatic with a color distinct from $c_1$; if they were monochromatic with $c_1$, this would contradict the maximality of $X$, and if they were not monochromatic, then $F$ would contain an element in $\mathcal{H}(2,1,0)$ or $\mathcal{H}(1,1,1)$ as a subcoloring, contradicting the assumption that $F_1$ is $\varepsilon_1$-standard.
    
    If there does \emph{not} exists an edge $e_0 \in y \ast X$ satisfying $F(e_0) = c_1$, then all edges in $y \ast X$ must be monochromatic with a color distinct from $c_1$; if they were monochromatic with $c_1$, this would again contradict the maximality of $X$, and if they were not monochromatic, then by the pigeonhole principle $F$ would contain an element in $\mathcal{H}(0,2,1)$ since the cardinality of $X$ is at least $c+1$, again contradicting the assumption that $F_1$ is $\varepsilon_1$-standard.
nodes.statement_short: Case on whether a $c_1$-edge exists; otherwise maximality of $X$ or a forbidden $\mathcal H$-configuration arises.

nodes.name: Intersections of maximal monochromatic cliques
nodes.statement:
Let $F$ be standard. 
For given distinct sets $X_1,X_2\in\mathcal{X}_F$ respectively corresponding to maximal cliques that are monochromatic with colors $c_1$ and $c_2$, the following holds:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $X_1\cap X_2 = \varnothing$, then $c_1 = c_2$ and there exists a matching  $M\subseteq X_1\ast X_2$ such that all edges in $M$ have color $c_1=c_2$ and all edges in $X_1\ast X_2 \setminus M$ have the same color $c_3$ that is distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$.
        \item If $X_1\cap X_2= \{v\}$, then $c_1 = c_2$ and all edges in $(X_1\setminus \{v\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v\})$ have the same color $c_3$ that is distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$.
        \item $|X_1\cap X_2| \geq 2$ cannot occur.
    \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Two maximal cliques are disjoint (joined by a matching plus a third color) or meet in one vertex, with equal colors.
assumptions: distinct sets $X_1,X_2\in\mathcal{X}_F$ respectively corresponding to maximal cliques that are monochromatic with colors $c_1$ and $c_2$

conclusions: $c_1 = c_2$ and there exists a matching  $M\subseteq X_1\ast X_2$ such that all edges in $M$ have color $c_1=c_2$ and all edges in $X_1\ast X_2 \setminus M$ have the same color $c_3$ that is distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$
$c_1 = c_2$ and all edges in $(X_1\setminus \{v\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v\})$ have the same color $c_3$ that is distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$

$c_1 = c_2$ and there exists a matching  $M\subseteq X_1\ast X_2$ such that all edges in $M$ have color $c_1=c_2$ and all edges in $X_1\ast X_2 \setminus M$ have the same color $c_3$ that is distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$
$c_1 = c_2$ and all edges in $(X_1\setminus \{v\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v\})$ have the same color $c_3$ that is distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$
nodes.label: lem:Claim_4

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5.6
nodes.statement:
Assume that $X_1\cap X_2 = \varnothing$. By \cref{lem:Claim_2}, there exists two sets $M_1, M_2\subseteq X_1 \ast X_2$ of edges satisfying $|M_2(x_1)| \le 1$ for any $x_1 \in X_1$ and $|M_1(x_2)| \le 1$ for any $x_2 \in X_2$  that are, respectively, all colored with color $c_1$ and $c_2$.

    
    If $c_1\ne c_2$, let us assume that $M_1$ is non-empty and pick some arbitrary edge $\{v_1,v_2\}\in M_1$ with $v_1\in X_1$ and $v_2\in X_2$. Applying \cref{lem:Claim_2} to $X_2$ and $v_1$ implies that that
    \[
        M_1 \supseteq v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1)).
    \]
    with $|M_2(v_1)| \le 1$.
    Since $|M_1(x_2)|\le 1$ for all $x_2\in X_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2}, it follows that there can exist at most one additional edge in $M_1$ that is not in $v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1))$, namely $\{M_2(v_1), z\}$ for some $z\in X_1\setminus v_1$. This however would likewise imply that $M_1 \supseteq z \ast (X_2 \setminus M_2(z))$ with $|M_2(z)| \le 1$, contradicting that $|M_1| \leq |X_2|$. Hence either $M_1 = \emptyset$ or
    \[
        M_1 = v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1))
    \]
    and by symmetry either $M_2 = \emptyset$ or 
    \[
        M_2 = (X_1\setminus M_1(v_2)) \ast v_2,
    \]
    for some $v_2 \in X_2$.
    It follows that there exists $v_ \in X_1$ and $v_2 \in X_2$ such that
    
    \begin{equation*}
        (X_1\setminus\{v_1\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v_2 \}) \subseteq X_1 \ast X_2 \setminus (M_1 \cup M_2)
    \end{equation*}
    
    and all edges in $(X_1\setminus\{v_1\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v_2 \})$ need to have the same color $c_3$ distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2} and symmetry. Then however, since we are assuming that $c_1 \neq c_2$, we get the contradiction that $p(\hat K_{3,3}; F) > 0$.
    
    If $c_1=c_2$, then $M_1 = M_2$ needs to be a matching by symmetry and $(X_1\ast X_2)\setminus (M_1\cup M_2)$ is again monochromatic with a color distinct from $c_1=c_2$.
    
    \medskip
    
    Assume now that $|X_1\cap X_2| = \{v\}$ and pick an arbitrary $w \in X_2 \setminus X_1$. Then $\{v,w\}$ has color $c_2$ and so all edges in $w \ast (X_1 \setminus \{v\})$ have the same color $c_3$ distinct from $c_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2}. By symmetry, the same argument is true for edges going from any $w\in X_1\setminus X_2$ to the set $X_2\setminus \{v\}$ with the color being distinct from $c_1$. Since $(X_1\setminus \{v\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v\})$ is a complete bipartite graph, the symmetry also implies that the color $c_3$ is the same for each choice of $w$, so that all edges in $(X_1\setminus \{v\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v\})$ have the same color $c_3$ distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$. Finally, if $c_1 \ne c_2$, we would get a contradiction to the assumption that $p(\hat K_{3,3};F) = 0$.

    \medskip
    
    Finally, if $|X_1\cap X_2| \ge 2$, then there exist $v_1, v_2 \in X_1\cap X_2$ and the edge $\{v_1, v_2\}$ therefore has both colors $c_1$ and $c_2$, implying that $c_1 = c_2$. By assumption $X_1 \neq X_2$, so there exists $v\in X_1\Delta X_2$. Let us w.l.o.g. say that $v\in X_2$. Then, for each $w \in X_1 \cap X_2$, of which there are at least two, the edge $\{v,w\}$ as color $c_1$, contradicting \cref{lem:Claim_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on $|X_1\cap X_2|$ using Claim 5.5; mixed colors force a $\hat K_{3,3}$ configuration.

nodes.name: Reduced looped coloring E_F
nodes.statement:
For a standard $F$, let us therefore construct
a $c$-coloring $E_F$ of the complete and partially looped graph on vertex set 
$\mathcal{X}_F\sqcup Y_F$, where $Y_F= \{ \{y\} \mid y \in V(F)\setminus 
\bigcup_{X \in \mathcal{X}_F} X\}$. Given $X, X_1, X_2 \in \mathcal{X}_F$ and $y \in Y_F$, we note that the edges in $y \ast X$ and $X_1 \ast X_2$ always have a clearly defined majority color in $F$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2} and \cref{lem:Claim_4}. The edges and their color in $E_F$ are now defined through 

\begin{equation} E_F(\{v_1, v_2\}) = \left\{\begin{array}{lr}
        \text{no edge} & \text{if } v_1 = v_2 \in Y_F, \\
        F(\{v_1, v_2\}) & \text{if } v_1 \neq v_2 \in Y_F, \\
        \text{color of } F[v_1]  & \text{if } v_1 = v_2 \in \mathcal{X}_F, \\
        \text{majority color in } v_1 \ast v_2 & \text{otherwise}. 
        \end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Contract each maximal monochromatic clique of $F$ to a looped vertex, keep the other vertices, and color by majority.

nodes.name: Definition of E_F (5.3)
nodes.statement:
E_F(\{v_1, v_2\}) = \left\{\begin{array}{lr}
        \text{no edge} & \text{if } v_1 = v_2 \in Y_F, \\
        F(\{v_1, v_2\}) & \text{if } v_1 \neq v_2 \in Y_F, \\
        \text{color of } F[v_1]  & \text{if } v_1 = v_2 \in \mathcal{X}_F, \\
        \text{majority color in } v_1 \ast v_2 & \text{otherwise}. 
        \end{array}\right.
nodes.label: eq:def_of_looped_graph_E

nodes.name: E_F has no large monochromatic cliques
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be standard. Given any $i\in [c]$, the only embeddings of $K_{\max(c+1,6)}^i$ in $E_F$ map everything to a single vertex. The same holds for $K_3^i$ if the embedding contains at least one vertex in $\mathcal{X}_F$.
conclusions: the only embeddings of $K_{\max(c+1,6)}^i$ in $E_F$ map everything to a single vertex
The same holds for $K_3^i$ if the embedding contains at least one vertex in $\mathcal{X}_F$
nodes.label: lem:standard_has_partition

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5.7
nodes.statement_short: Rule out monochromatic triangles through a clique vertex via an $\mathcal H(2,1,0)$ configuration, then deduce the clique statement.

nodes.name: Standard flags are blow-ups of Ramsey colorings
nodes.statement:
Assume \boxedchar{A1} and that $F \in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing$ is a $(\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)$-standard flag of order $n_1 = v(F)$. We have $E_F\in\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}$ and $Y_F=\varnothing$ for \whiteboxedchar{$n_1$ sufficiently large} and for every $X\in\mathcal{X}_F$ we have
    \begin{equation} (1-\varepsilon_3) \, \frac{n_1}{R_{c-1}(3)-1}\le |X|
    \le  (1+\varepsilon_3) \, \frac{n_1}{R_{c-1}(3)-1}.      
    \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A near-optimal standard flag contracts to an extremal Ramsey looped coloring with balanced clique sizes.
assumptions: $F \in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing$ is a $(\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)$-standard flag of order $n_1 = v(F)$
nodes.label: lem:standard_is_Ramsey

nodes.name: Clique size bounds (5.4)
nodes.statement:
(1-\varepsilon_3) \, \frac{n_1}{R_{c-1}(3)-1}\le |X|
    \le  (1+\varepsilon_3) \, \frac{n_1}{R_{c-1}(3)-1}.
nodes.label: eq:first_bound_on_cliques

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.8
nodes.statement_short: Count triangles inside cliques: too few cliques exceed the Ramsey upper bound, too many contradict triangle-freeness; then exclude $Y_F$.

nodes.name: Triangle density lower bound (5.5)
nodes.statement:
p(\hat K_3; F)
    \ge
    \frac{\sum_{X\in\mathcal{X}_F}\binom{X}{3}}{\binom{n_1}{3}} \geq ....
nodes.label: eq:first_bound_on_triangle_density

nodes.name: Random subsets embed with balanced parts
nodes.statement: Assume \boxedchar{A1} and that $F \in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing$ is a $(\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)$-standard flag of order $n_1 = v(F)$. With probability $1-\varepsilon_4§$ a uniformly chosen $n_2$-sized subset $\mathscr W \subseteq V(F)$ has an embedding $\varphi:V(\mathscr W)\to V(E_F)$ such that $|\varphi^{-1}(v)|/|\varphi^{-1}(w)| \ge 1-\varepsilon_4$ for all $v,w\in V(E_F)$.
assumptions: $F \in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing$ is a $(\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)$-standard flag of order $n_1 = v(F)$
conclusions: With probability $1-\varepsilon_4§$ a uniformly chosen $n_2$-sized subset $\mathscr W \subseteq V(F)$ has an embedding $\varphi:V(\mathscr W)\to V(E_F)$ such that $|\varphi^{-1}(v)|/|\varphi^{-1}(w)| \ge 1-\varepsilon_4$ for all $v,w\in V(E_F)$
nodes.label: lem:standard_has_uniform_subgraph

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.9
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over three failure events, bounded by Boole's inequality and Chernoff-Hoeffding.

nodes.name: Bound on P_3 (5.7)
nodes.statement: P_3 \leq \frac{1}{P_I}\binom{n_2}{2}\frac{|M|}{\binom{n_1}{2}} \leq \varepsilon_4/3
nodes.label: eq:p3

nodes.name: Smallness of epsilon_1
nodes.statement: Assume that \whiteboxedchar{$\varepsilon_1$ is small enough} to satisfy $(1 + 1/s) \, \varepsilon_1 \le \varepsilon_4 / 2$.

nodes.name: Assumption A4 and r
nodes.statement:
Let us also write $r=R_{c-1}(3)-1$ and add an additional assumption to the list in the form of

\begin{itemize} \itemsep0em 
    \item[\boxedchar{A4}] $p(\hat K_3; G)$ is small enough such that the bound in \cref{lem:Claim_1} is at least $1 - \varepsilon_4$.
nodes.statement_short: Sets $r=R_{c-1}(3)-1$ and assumes $p(\hat K_3;G)$ is small enough for Lemma 5.4's bound to be at least $1-\varepsilon_4$.

nodes.name: A typical set W with an embedding into E
nodes.statement:
Assume \boxedchar{A1}, \boxedchar{A3}, and \boxedchar{A4}. 
    There exists a set $W \subseteq V(G)$ with $|W| = n_2$ with a partition $W = C_1 \cup \ldots \cup C_{r}$ 
   satisfying 
    $|C_i| / |C_j| \ge 1-\varepsilon_4$ 
    as well as some unique $E\in\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}$ 
    such that for any $x,y\in V(G)$ chosen uniformly at random,  with probability at least $1-\varepsilon_5$ the induced sub-coloring $G[W \cup \{x, y\}]$ embeds into $E$.
nodes.statement_short: Some $n_2$-set $W$ with balanced parts embeds into a unique $E\in\mathcal L_{ex}$, and so does $W$ plus two random vertices w.h.p.
nodes.label: lem:Claim_7

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.10
nodes.statement:
If $\mathscr U$ is a uniform random subsets of $G$ of size $n_2$, and for each $F\in\mathcal{F}^\varnothing_{n_1}$, $\mathscr W_F$ is a uniform random subset of $F$ of size $n_2$ then we get
    
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P[G[\mathscr U]\text{ embeds into some $\mathcal{L}^{(c)}_{\operatorname{ex}}$}]
        &\ge
        \sum_{\substack{F\in\mathcal{F}_{n_1}^\varnothing\\ F\text{ is $\varepsilon_1$-standard}}} \mathbb P[G[\mathscr W_F]\text{ embeds into } E_F] \, p(F;G) \\
        &\ge(1-\varepsilon_4)^2 \ge 1-2\varepsilon_4,
    \end{align*}
    
    where the first inequality follows by \cref{lemma:double_counting}, the second inequality follow from \cref{lem:standard_has_uniform_subgraph}, \cref{lem:Claim_1} and \boxedchar{A4}, and the last inequality simply omits the quadratic term. Note that the same also holds if $\mathscr U$ is of size $n_2 +1$ and $n_2 + 2$, assuming \whiteboxedchar{$n_1$, $n_2$, and $\varepsilon_3$} are adjusted accordingly.

    Let $\mathscr W$ be an  $n_2$-sized subset of $G$ chosen uniformly at random and let $\mathscr P_1$ and $\mathscr P_2$ be two vertices in $V(G)$ also chosen uniformly at random. Note that $\mathscr W$, $\mathscr P_1$, and $\mathscr P_2$ are independent and let the following five events partition our probability space
    
    \begin{align*}
        I_1 &= \{\mathscr P_1\in \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \in \mathscr W\}, \\
        I_2 &= \{\mathscr P_1\in \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \notin \mathscr W\}, \\
        I_3 &= \{\mathscr P_1\notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \in \mathscr W\}, \\
        I_4 &= \{\mathscr P_1\notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_1 = \mathscr P_2\}, \text{ and} \\
        I_5 &= \{\mathscr P_1\notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_1 \ne \mathscr P_2\} .
    \end{align*}
    Then $\mathscr W \cup \{\mathscr P_1, \mathscr P_2\}$ is a uniform random $n_2$-sized set when conditioned on $I_1$, uniform random $(n_2+1)$-sized set when conditioned on $I_2,I_3$ or $I_4$ and a random $(n_2+2)$-sized subset when conditioned on $I_5$.
    
    It follows that
    \begin{align*}
    &\mathbb P[\mathscr W \cup \{\mathscr P_1, \mathscr P_2\}\text{ embeds into some }\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}]\\
    &=
    \sum_{i=1,\dots,5} \mathbb P[(\mathscr W \cup \{\mathscr P_1, \mathscr P_2\} \text{ embeds into some } \mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}) \text{ and } I_i \text{ holds} \} \ge 1 - 10\varepsilon_4
    \end{align*}
    due to the oberservation at the beginning of this proof. It follows that there
    exists at least one set $W$ with $|W|=n_2$ so that
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb P[\mathscr W \cup \{\mathscr P_1, \mathscr P_2\}\text{ embeds into some }\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}, \mathscr W = W] \ge 1 - 10\varepsilon_4   
    \end{align*}
    We assume that \whiteboxedchar{$\varepsilon_4$ is sufficiently small} so that we get the lower bound $\ge 1-\varepsilon_5$. When \whiteboxedchar{$n_2$ is sufficiently large}, there exists exactly one $E\in\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}$ into which $G[W]$ embeds, proving the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Average over random $n_1$-subsets (Lemmas 5.4, 5.9), then condition on how two random vertices meet a random $W$ and fix a good $W$.

nodes.name: Fixed set W_G with partition and E
nodes.statement: Assuming \boxedchar{A1}, \boxedchar{A3} and \boxedchar{A4}, fix a set $W_G \subseteq V(G)$ as guaranteed by \cref{lem:Claim_7} together with a partition $C_1,...,C_r$ and $E \in \mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}$ be the looped graph associated with $G[W]$.

nodes.name: Identification V(E)=[r]
nodes.statement: Let us w.l.o.g. assume that $V(E) = [r]$ and that each of the components $C_i$ correspond to the vertex $i$ in $E$.

nodes.name: Sets E_0, V_0, F_i, V_i
nodes.statement:
Now let
\begin{equation}
    \begin{aligned}
        E_{0} &= 
        \{(u,v)\in V(G)\times V(G) \mid G[W_G\cup\{u,v\}]\text{ does not embed into } E\}, \\
        V_{0} &= \{v\in V(G)  \mid v\text{ is incident to }\ge
        \varepsilon_6n_0 \text{ edges in }E_0\}, \\
        F_i &= \{v\in V(G)\setminus V_0  \mid W_G\cup \{v\} \text{ embeds into }E \}, \text{ and} \\
        V_i & = \left\{  v\in V(G)  \mid \ v\ast F_j
        \text{ has }\ge\delta_0 |F_j|\text{ edges with color }E(\{i,j\}) \text{ for each }j\in [r]  \right\}.
    \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bad pairs $E_0$, high bad-degree vertices $V_0$, vertices $F_i$ embedding as part $i$, and vertices $V_i$ colored like part $i$.

nodes.name: Definition of E_0, V_0, F_i, V_i (5.8)
nodes.statement:
\begin{aligned}
        E_{0} &= 
        \{(u,v)\in V(G)\times V(G) \mid G[W_G\cup\{u,v\}]\text{ does not embed into } E\}, \\
        V_{0} &= \{v\in V(G)  \mid v\text{ is incident to }\ge
        \varepsilon_6n_0 \text{ edges in }E_0\}, \\
        F_i &= \{v\in V(G)\setminus V_0  \mid W_G\cup \{v\} \text{ embeds into }E \}, \text{ and} \\
        V_i & = \left\{  v\in V(G)  \mid \ v\ast F_j
        \text{ has }\ge\delta_0 |F_j|\text{ edges with color }E(\{i,j\}) \text{ for each }j\in [r]  \right\}.
    \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:E0V0FiVi

nodes.name: Bounds on E_0 and V_0
nodes.statement:
Assume \boxedchar{A3} and \boxedchar{A4}.
    We have $|E_0|<\varepsilon_5 n_0^2$ and $|V_0|\le \varepsilon_6n_0$.
nodes.label: lem:bound_for_zerosets

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.11
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lem:Claim_7} we have $|E_0|\le \varepsilon_5n_0^2$.
    Furthermore, the definition of $V_0$ implies the bound $\varepsilon_6n_0|V_0|\le 2|E_0|$ which gives the claim for $V_0$ when \whiteboxedchar{$\varepsilon_5$ is sufficiently small}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.10 bounds $E_0$; double counting bounds $V_0$.

nodes.name: Sizes and disjointness of the parts F_i and V_i
nodes.statement: Assume \boxedchar{A3} and \boxedchar{A4}. For every $i\in [r]$ we have $|F_i| \geq (1-\varepsilon_7) \, n /r$, the $V_i$ are pairwise disjoint and we have $F_i\subseteq V_i$.
nodes.label: lem:Claim_8

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.12
nodes.statement:
First, note that
    
    \begin{equation} \Big|V(G) \setminus \big(V_0 \cup \bigcup_{i=1}^r F_i \big)\Big|^2\le |E_0|.
    \end{equation}
    
    Now, assume that for some $i$ we have
    $|F_i|<(1-\varepsilon_7) \, n / r$.
    Then by \cref{eq:crude_upper_bound_on_remainder}, the union $\bigcup_{i\ne j} F_j$ has size
    at least
    \[
       \Big|\bigcup_{i\ne j} F_j \Big| \ge n -  |V_0| - \sqrt{|E_0|} - |F_i|
       \ge
       \left( 1-\varepsilon_6 - \sqrt{\varepsilon_5} - \frac{1-\varepsilon_7}{{r}} \right)\, n
    \]
    by \cref{lem:bound_for_zerosets}.
    The number of monochromatic triangles of $G$ is at least
    \[
        \binom{|F_i|}{3}
        - n|E_0|
        + \sum_{j \neq i} \binom{|F_j|}{3} \geq \binom{|F_i|}{3}
        - n|E_0|
        + (r-1)
        \binom{\frac{1}{r-1}|\bigcup_{i \ne j} F_j|}{3}
    \]
    and therefore for \whiteboxedchar{$\varepsilon_4$, $\varepsilon_5$ and $\varepsilon_6$ sufficiently small } as well as \whiteboxedchar{$n_0$ sufficiently large} and $n\ge n_0$ we would get a contradiction to \boxedchar{A4} since $p(\hat K_3; G)\ge  \varsigma+\varepsilon_4/2$.
    
    
    Note that in particular the $F_i$ are non-empty for \whiteboxedchar{$n_0$ sufficiently large}.

    Now let us show that the sets $V_i$ are disjoint when \whiteboxedchar{$\delta_0 > 1/2$}. Otherwise, let $v \in V_i \cap V_j$ for some $i \neq j$ and note that would have at least $\delta_0|F_i|$ edges with color $E(\{i,j\})$ and $\delta_0|F_i|$ edges with color $E(\{i\})$ in $v\ast F_i$ with colors. However, by \cref{lem:standard_is_Ramsey}, loops in $E$ have a different color from their incident edges in $E$, a contradiction, since $F_i$ is non-empty and $\delta_0 > 1/2$. 

    Now let us show that $F_i\subseteq V_i$. For any $v\in F_i$ we know that $v\not\in V_0$, so that $|E_0(v)|<\varepsilon_6n_0$. Therefore, for each $j$ we have
    \[
        \frac{|\{w\in F_j\mid G(\{v,w\})\ne E(\{i,j\}) \}|}{|F_i|}
        \le 
        \frac{|E_0(v)|}{|F_i|}
        \le
        \varepsilon_6 \left(\frac{1-\varepsilon_7}{r}\right)^{-1}.
    \]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.13
nodes.statement:
Let $\phi_0\in\operatorname{Hom}^+(\mathcal{A}^\varnothing, \mathbb R)$ be an arbitrary but fixed extremal positive homomorphism for $\hat K_3-\varsigma$, that is $\phi_0(\hat K_3-\varsigma)=0$. By \boxedchar{A2} we therefore also have $\phi_0(\hat K_{3,1}+\hat K_{3,3})=0$. Denote by $\mathcal{H}$ all flags corresponding to summands in $\hat K_{3,1}$ or $\hat K_{3,3}$. Let us sketch the argument that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}^\varnothing \cong \mathcal{A}^\varnothing / \langle \mathcal{H}\rangle$. There is an algebra homomorphism $\pi: \mathcal{A}^\varnothing \to \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}^\varnothing$ defined by mapping a flag $F\in \mathcal{F}$ to $F$ if $F\in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing_{\mathcal{H}}$ and otherwise to 0, see \cite{Razborov_2007} Definition 4 and Theorem 2.6. Clearly, it is surjective and $\langle \mathcal{H} \rangle$ is in its kernel. To see that its kernel is exactly $\langle \mathcal{H} \rangle$ we notice that if $\pi(f)=0$ then $\pi(f)$ may be written as a linear combination of elements of $\mathcal{K}^\varnothing_{\mathcal{H}}$. But we can pull back this linear combination to a linear combination of $\mathcal{K}^\varnothing$ and then it follows that $f$ is in $\langle \mathcal{H}\rangle$.

    Since $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}^\varnothing \cong \mathcal{A}^\varnothing / \langle \mathcal{H}\rangle$,
    the map $\phi_0$ also induces a positive homomorphism of $\mathcal{A}^\varnothing_{\mathcal{H}}$. Hence, by \cref{thm:homfunctional} there exists a sequence $F_i$ of $\alpha_i$-standard flags with $\lim_{i\to\infty}\alpha_i=\varsigma$ in $\mathcal{A}^\varnothing_{\mathcal{H}}$, and therefore in $\mathcal{A}^\varnothing$, satisfying $\lim_{i \to \infty} p(F;F_i) = \phi_0(F)$. By \cref{lem:standard_is_Ramsey}, the $\hat K_3$ density in $F_i$ is asymptotically $1/(R_{c-1}(3)-1)^{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: An extremal homomorphism lives in the algebra forbidding $\mathcal H$; realize it by standard flags and apply Proposition 5.8.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5.17
nodes.statement:
Recoloring any individual edge $\{v,w\} \in G[V_i]$ with $G(\{v,w\}) \neq E(\{i\})$ to the correct color creates no more than
    
    \begin{align*}
       &|V^\ast|+|V_i| + \sum_{j \neq i} (|V_j|-|F_j|) + |F_j|(1-\delta_0) \le \left(1 - \delta_0\left(1-\frac{1}{r}\right)(1-\varepsilon_7)\right)n 
    \end{align*}
    new monochromatic triangles, where we have used \cref{lem:Claim_8} to lower bound the $|F_j|$.



























       




    
    On the other hand, the number of destroyed triangles is at least
    \[
        \sum_{\substack{j \neq i\\E(\{i,j\})=G(\{v,w\})}}
        (2\delta_0-1)|F_j|
        \ge 2(2\delta_0-1)\frac{1-\varepsilon_7}{r}n,
    \]
    where we have used \cref{lem:Degree_at_lest_two} so that the summation has at least two summands as well as \cref{lem:Claim_8} to lower bound the $|F_j|$.
    The difference
    between the destroyed and created triangles
    is therefore at least
    
    \begin{align*}
         &\left((4\delta_0-2)\frac{1-\varepsilon_7}{r}-1 + \delta_0\left(1-\frac{1}{r}\right)(1-\varepsilon_7)\right)n \\
         &=\left(\delta_0-1+\frac{5\delta_0-2}{r}+\left(-\delta_0\left(1-\frac{1}{r}\right) -\frac{4\delta_0-2}{r} \right)\varepsilon_7 \right)n \ge \frac{n}{r}
    \end{align*}
    where the lower bound holds for \whiteboxedchar{sufficiently large $\delta_0$} and \whiteboxedchar{sufficiently small $\varepsilon_7$}. Recoloring more than 
    $r\binom{n}{2}(p(\hat K_3,G)-\varsigma_n)/3$ edges would therefore destroy more than $\binom{n}{3}(p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma_n)$ triangles, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Each wrongly colored edge in $V_i$ destroys more triangles than recoloring creates, so many such edges contradict near-optimality.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5.19
nodes.statement:
Let $(x,y)\in E^\ast$ with $x\in V_i$, $y\in V_j$ and $E(\{x,y\})$ is not the loop color of $E$. By
    \cref{lem:exists_cherry_in_Ramsey} there exists at least one
    $k$ so that $E(\{i,k\}) = E(\{j,k\})=G(\{x,y\})$. By
    definition of $V_i$, both $x\ast F_k$ and $y\ast F_k$
    each have more than $\delta_0 |F_k|$ edges with color $G(\{x,y\})$ in $F_k$.
    Therefore, there are at least 
    \[
        (2\delta_0-1)|F_k|\ge (2\delta_0-1)\frac{1-\varepsilon_7}{r}n\ge (2\delta_0-1)\frac{1}{r+1}n
    \]
    monochromatic
    triangles containing $\{x,y\}$, where we have used \cref{lem:Claim_8} to lower bound $|F_k|$ and assume that \whiteboxedchar{$\varepsilon_7$ is sufficiently small} for the second inequality to hold. Note that each choice of $(x,y) \in
    E^\ast$ dictates its own set of of such monochromatic triangles, so we can sum them up without overcounting. If more than
    $\frac{r+1}{2\delta_0-1}(p(\hat K_3; G)-\varsigma_n)\binom{n}{2}/3$
    of these edges were to exist, they would lead to a decrease of the monochromatic triangle count of more than $(p(\hat K_3,G)-\varsigma_n)\binom{n}{3}$,
    a contradiction. Note that recoloring all of these edges $\{x,y\}$ respectively to $E(\{i,j\})$ \emph{simultaneously} does not create any additional triangles. Indeed, after recoloring, the only triangles left are those with the loop color. But we did not change any edge to the loop color and therefore we did not add any triangles. This establishes the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Each non-loop error edge lies in many monochromatic triangles via a cherry (Lemma 5.16); recoloring them simultaneously creates none.

nodes.name: Avenues to an equivalence of Ramsey number and multiplicity
nodes.statement:
While in our case the colorings were both known and crucial in order to derive an exact rather than a floating point-based flag algebra certificate, \cref{th:stability}, which draws a connection between the Ramsey number $R_{c-1}(3)$ and the Ramsey multiplicity problem $m_c(3)$, in theory opens up an avenue to establish a sort of equivalence of the two problems without first explicitly solving both or even either problem: 

\begin{itemize} \setlength\itemsep{0em}
    \item[1)] We could derive a flag algebra certificate for a particular $c > 4$ establishing $m_c(3)$ and meeting the requirements of \cref{th:stability} without explicit knowledge of the $R_{c-1}(3)$-Ramsey colorings. Note that this would imply the exact value of $R_{c-1}(3) = m_c(3)^{-1/2} - 1$.
    \item[2)] We could show that the Ramsey multiplicity problem satisfies the requirements of \cref{th:stability} for arbitrary $c \geq 3$, in particular that $\hat K_{3,1}$ and $\hat K_{3,3}$ have zero density in an extremal construction, through a purely theoretical argument not relying on the semidefinite programming method and without explicitly determining $m_c(3)$. This would imply that $m_c(3) = (R_{c-1}(3) - 1)^{-2}$ without giving us explicit knowledge of either value.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 5.2 could determine $R_{c-1}(3)$ from a certificate, or $m_c(3)$ from a theoretical argument, without knowing either.

nodes.name: Ramsey multiplicity of triangles equals inverse squared Ramsey bound
nodes.statement: For any $c \geq 3$, we have $m_c(3) = (R_{c-1}(3) - 1)^{-2}$ and the only extremal constructions are derived from $R_{c-1}(3)$-Ramsey colorings.
nodes.statement_short: For all $c\ge3$, $m_c(3)=(R_{c-1}(3)-1)^{-2}$ with extremal constructions from Ramsey colorings.
conclusions: the only extremal constructions are derived from $R_{c-1}(3)$-Ramsey colorings
