nodes.name: Ramsey colorings share no (r-1)-subcolorings
nodes.statement: Suppose that for some $c\ge 3$ we have actually established that $\hat K_{3,1}$ and $\hat K_{3,3}$ have zero density in any extremal construction. Then, aside from establishing \cref{conj:equivalence} for that particular $c$, this would also imply that any two distinct $c$-color Ramsey-colorings $R_1, R_2$ cannot share any $r-1$-sized subcolorings.
assumptions: for some $c\ge 3$ we have actually established that $\hat K_{3,1}$ and $\hat K_{3,3}$ have zero density in any extremal construction
conclusions: any two distinct $c$-color Ramsey-colorings $R_1, R_2$ cannot share any $r-1$-sized subcolorings

nodes.name: Argument for Claim on shared subcolorings
nodes.statement: This follows since otherwise we could, just as in \cref{sec:Ramsey_mult_graphs}, consider a looped coloring $E$ on $R_1\cup \{v_2\}$ with $E(\{v_2\})=E(\{v_1,v_2\})=E(\{v_1\})$ so that $E[V(R_1)\setminus \{v_1\}]\simeq R_2$. By choosing a weighting on $E$ where every $v\in V(E)$ has weight $\frac{1}{r}$ except for $v_1$ and $v_2$ which get the weight $\frac{1}{2r}$, we would have a weighted looped coloring achieving a monochromatic triangle density of $\varsigma$ with a non-zero $\hat K_{3,1}$ density.
nodes.statement_short: Glue two Ramsey colorings sharing an $(r-1)$-subcoloring into a weighted looped coloring attaining $\varsigma$ with positive $\hat K_{3,1}$ density.

nodes.statement:
For each $S \in\mathbf S(F'; F)$ let $\iota_S: V(F') \overset{\sim}{\hookrightarrow} S \subseteq V(G)$ be an arbitrary but fixed bijection.
        There is a natural map $\mathbf{S}(F_1,\dots,F_\ell; F') \times \mathbf{S}(F'; F) \to \mathbf{S}(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F)$ given by mapping $(S_1,\dots,S_\ell)\in \mathbf S(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F')$ and $S \in \mathbf{S}(F'; F)$ to $(\iota_S(S_1),\dots,\iota_S(S_\ell))$. This map is surjective and the pre-image of every point is of equal cardinality.

nodes.name: Conclude by double counting over fibres
nodes.statement: Since any $(S_1,\dots, S_\ell)\in\mathbf S(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F)$ satisfies $F[S_i]\simeq F_i$  for all $1\le i\le \ell$ if and only if all elements $(S_1',\dots,S_\ell)'\in \mathbf S(F_1,\dots,F_\ell;F')$ and $S \in \mathbf{S}(F'; F)$ in its pre-image also satisfy $F[S] \simeq F'$ as well as $F'[S_i']\simeq F_i$ for all $1\le i\le \ell$,  the desired statement follows.

nodes.name: Approximate $f$ by flag combinations with densities at least
nodes.statement:
For each $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an integer $n_0 = n_0(f, \varepsilon)$ such that $f$ can be expressed as a linear combination of elements in $\mathcal{F}^\tau_{n}$ while also satisfying
    $p(f,F)\ge -\varepsilon$ and therefore $p(f+\varepsilon,F)\ge 0$ for  any $F\in \mathcal{F}^\tau_{n}$ with $n \geq n_0$. 
    Otherwise, there would exist a positive homomorphism $\phi$ by \cref{thm:homfunctional} satisfying $\phi(f)<-\varepsilon$, contradicting the assumption that $f$ is a positive element.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $f$ by flag combinations with densities at least $-\varepsilon$, via Theorem 3.3

nodes.name: Push the bound down with the linear downward operator
nodes.statement:
We now have
    \[
    \llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau+\varepsilon \cdot q_{\tau}(\tau)
    \ge
    \llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau +\varepsilon \cdot q_{\tau}(\tau) \cdot \tau\vert_\tau 
    =
    \llbracket f+\varepsilon \rrbracket_\tau
    =
    \sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}^\tau_{n}} p(f+\varepsilon,F) \, \llbracket F\rrbracket_\tau
    \ge 0,
    \]
    where in the first and last step we have used that $0 = 0 \cdot \varnothing \leq \tau\vert_\tau  \leq 1 \cdot \varnothing = 1$, which is in fact true for any flag in $\mathcal{F}^\varnothing$, and then for the second and third step, respectively, the linearity of the downward operator and the fact that f, and therefore also $f + \varepsilon$, is expressible as a linear combination of elements in $\mathcal{F}_{n}^\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Push the bound down with the linear downward operator

nodes.name: Let $\varepsilon\to 0$
nodes.statement: Since $q_\tau(\tau)$ is a constant, it follows that $\llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau \geq -\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and hence $\llbracket f\rrbracket_\tau \geq 0$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Let $\varepsilon\to 0$

nodes.name: Density invariance holds for flags
nodes.statement:
We start by noting that \cref{eq:density_permutation} holds for \emph{flags} $F_1, \ldots, F_\ell \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$,
    
    since for any $i\in \{1,\dots,\ell\}$ and $(S_1, \ldots, S_\ell) \in {\bf S}(F_1, \ldots, F_\ell; F)$ we have $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)\vert_{S_i} \simeq \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_i)$ if and only if $F\vert_{S_i} \simeq F_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Density invariance holds for flags

nodes.name: Kernel preserved and product commutes on flags
nodes.statement:
Using this, it immediately follows that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\mathcal{K}^\tau) \subseteq \mathcal{K}^{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}$ and that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}$ likewise commutes with the multiplication of flags, since for $F_1, F_2\in\mathcal{F}^\tau$ we have
    
    \begin{align*}
        \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1\cdot F_2) & = \sum_{H\in\mathcal{F}_n^\tau} p(F_1,F_2;H) \, \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(H) \\
        & = \sum_{H\in\mathcal{F}_n^\tau} p(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1),\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_2);\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(H)) \, \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(H) \\
        & = \sum_{H \in \mathcal{F}_n^{\pi^{\alpha, \beta}(\tau)}}  p(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1),\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_2);H) \, H \\
        & = \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_1)\cdot\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F_2)
    \end{align*}
    
    for some large enough $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel preserved and product commutes on flags

nodes.name: Extend by linearity
nodes.statement: It follows that the linear extension of $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}$ induces an algebra homomorphism from $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ to $\mathcal{A}^{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}$ and that \cref{eq:product_commute} as well as \cref{eq:density_permutation} hold for arbitrary algebra elements by linearity.
nodes.statement_short: Extend by linearity

nodes.name: Prove the identity for single flags
nodes.statement:
Let us first show that the statement is true for any flag $F = (G,\psi) \in \mathcal{F}^\tau$. We note that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)\vert_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} = (\alpha\circ G,\varnothing) = \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}(F\vert_\tau)$. For the coefficient, we likewise have
    
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        q_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F))
        &=&
        \frac{|\{\varphi : [v(\tau)] \hookrightarrow V(G) \mid (\alpha\circ G, \varphi\circ \beta) \simeq (\alpha\circ G,\psi\circ \beta) \}|}{v(G)! \, / \, (v(G)-v(\tau))!},
    \end{eqnarray*}
    
    since $(\alpha\circ G,\varphi\circ \beta) \simeq (\alpha\circ G,\psi\circ \beta)$ if and only if $(G,\varphi) \simeq F$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the identity for single flags

nodes.name: Unlabelled flags agree
nodes.statement: We note that $\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)\vert_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} = (\alpha\circ G,\varnothing) = \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}(F\vert_\tau)$.
nodes.statement_short: Unlabelled flags agree

nodes.name: Coefficients $q$ agree
nodes.statement:
For the coefficient, we likewise have
    
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        q_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F))
        &=&
        \frac{|\{\varphi : [v(\tau)] \hookrightarrow V(G) \mid (\alpha\circ G, \varphi\circ \beta) \simeq (\alpha\circ G,\psi\circ \beta) \}|}{v(G)! \, / \, (v(G)-v(\tau))!},
    \end{eqnarray*}
    
    since $(\alpha\circ G,\varphi\circ \beta) \simeq (\alpha\circ G,\psi\circ \beta)$ if and only if $(G,\varphi) \simeq F$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients $q$ agree

nodes.name: Combine into the downward identity for flags
nodes.statement:
It follows that 
    
    \begin{align*}
        \llbracket \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F) \rrbracket_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} & = q_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)}(\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)) \cdot \pi^{\alpha,\beta}(F)\vert_{\pi^{\alpha,\beta}(\tau)} \\
        
        
        
        & = q_\tau(F) \cdot \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}( F \vert_\tau )
        
        = \pi^{\alpha, \varnothing}\big( q_\tau(F) \cdot F \vert_\tau \big) \\
        
        & = \pi^{\alpha,\varnothing}(\llbracket F \rrbracket_{\tau}).
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Combine into the downward identity for flags

nodes.name: Extend by linearity
nodes.statement: The statement now follows for all elements in $\mathcal{A}^\tau$ by linearity.
nodes.statement_short: Extend by linearity

nodes.name: Prove the first equality entry-wise
nodes.statement:
Let $F_1, F_2 \in \mathcal{F}^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)}_N$. For the first equality, we have
    
    \begin{align*}
        (D_F^\tau)^{(\alpha, \beta)}_{F_1,F_2} &=
        (D_F^\tau)_{\pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_1), \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_2)} \\
        & = p \left( \big\llbracket \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_1) \cdot \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})}(F_2) \big\rrbracket_{\tau} ; F \right) \\
        & = p \left( \pi^{(\alpha, \varnothing)} \left( \big\llbracket \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})} (F_1 \cdot F_2) \big\rrbracket_{\tau} \right); \pi^{(\alpha, \varnothing)} (F) \right) \\
        & = p(\left\llbracket F_1 \cdot F_2 \right\rrbracket_{\pi^{(\alpha, \beta)}(\tau)}; \pi^{(\alpha, \varnothing)} (F)) \\
        & = \big( D_{\pi^{(\alpha,\varnothing)}(F)}^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)} \big)_{F_1,F_2}.
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Prove the first equality entry-wise

nodes.name: Prove the second equality by averaging, using Lemmas 4
nodes.statement:
For the second equality, we have
    
    \begin{align*}
        (\hat D^\tau_{F})^{(\alpha,\beta)}_{F_1,F_2} 
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} \left( D^\tau_{\pi^{(\alpha',\varnothing)} (F)} \right)^{(\alpha, \beta)}_{F_1, F_2} \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} p(\llbracket \pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \beta^{-1})}(F_1 \cdot F_2) \rrbracket_\tau; \pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)) \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon}  p(\pi^{(\alpha^{-1}, \varnothing)} (\llbracket (F_1 \cdot F_2) \rrbracket_{\pi^{(\alpha, \beta)} (\tau)} ); \pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)) \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} p(\left\llbracket F_1 \cdot F_2 \right\rrbracket_{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)}; \pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)) \\
        & = \frac{1}{|\Upsilon|}\sum_{\alpha' \in \Upsilon} \left( D^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)}_{\pi^{(\alpha', \varnothing)}(F)} \right)_{F_1, F_2} \\
        & = \big( \hat D_F^{\pi^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\tau)} \big)_{F_1, F_2}.
    \end{align*}
    
    Here we have made use of \cref{lemma:extend_color_vertex_permutations} as well as \cref{lemma:harmonic_downward} for both arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the second equality by averaging, using Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2

nodes.name: Expected densities in a random subset equal those in $G$
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lemma:double_counting}, we have both
    
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb E[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M])]
        =
        p(\hat K_3;G) \quad \text{and} \quad
        \mathbb E[p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3};G[\mathscr M])]
        =
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3};G).
    \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.2 Definition and existence of standard flags
nodes.statement_short: Expected densities in a random subset equal those in $G$

nodes.name: Bound the probability of too high triangle density
nodes.statement:
Let $x=\mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M])>\varsigma+\varepsilon_1]$ and note that, for \whiteboxedchar{sufficiently large $n_0$}, we have by \boxedchar{A1} that $p(\hat K_3; G)\ge \varsigma-\varepsilon_1^2$.
    By approximating $p(\hat K_3;G)$ through a step function, we have
    \[
    (\varsigma-\varepsilon_1^2) \, (1-x)
    +
    (\varsigma+\varepsilon_1) \, x  
    \le
    p(\hat K_3;G),
    \]
    and therefore
    
    \begin{equation} \mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M] > \varsigma + \varepsilon_1) = x
        \le
        \frac{p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma+\varepsilon_1^2}{\varepsilon_1(1+\varepsilon_1)}.
    \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5.2 Definition and existence of standard flags
nodes.statement_short: Bound the probability of too high triangle density

nodes.name: Markov's inequality for the forbidden configurations
nodes.statement:
Using Markov's inequality, we get
    
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P[ 
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; G[\mathscr M]) > 0] &\leq \mathbb P \left[p(\hat K_{3,1};G[\mathscr M]) \ge \binom{n_1}{4}^{-1} \right]
        +\mathbb P \left[p(\hat K_{3,3};G[\mathscr M]) \ge \binom{n_1}{6}^{-1} \right] \\ 
        &\le \binom{n_1}{4} \, p(\hat K_{3,1};G)
        +\binom{n_1}{6} \, p(\hat K_{3,3};G).
    \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.2 Definition and existence of standard flags
nodes.statement_short: Markov's inequality for the forbidden configurations

nodes.name: Use A2 to relate forbidden densities to excess triangle dens
nodes.section: 5.2 Definition and existence of standard flags
nodes.statement_short: Use A2 to relate forbidden densities to excess triangle density

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement:
Finally, through the union bound and by combining \cref{eq:k3bnd} as well as \cref{eq:k31k33bnd}, we therefore get
    
    \begin{align*}
        & \quad \mathbb P[G[\mathscr M] \text{ is } (\varsigma+\varepsilon_1)\text{-standard}] \\
        & = 1 - \mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M]) >  \varsigma+\varepsilon_1 \vee 
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; G[\mathscr M]) > 0] \\
        & \geq 1 - \mathbb P[p(\hat K_3;G[\mathscr M]) >  \varsigma+\varepsilon_1] - \mathbb P[ 
        p(\hat K_{3,1} + \hat K_{3,3}; G[\mathscr M]) > 0] \\
        & \geq 1 - \frac{p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma+\varepsilon_1^2}{\varepsilon_1(1+\varepsilon_1)} - \frac{\binom{n_1}{6}(p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma)+\varepsilon_1}{s} \\
        & = 1 - 
            \left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon_1(1+\varepsilon_1)} + \frac{\binom{n_1}{6}}{s} \right)
            \left(p(\hat K_3;G)-\varsigma\right)
            -
            \left( 
            \frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon_1}+\frac{1}{s}
            \right)
            \varepsilon_1,
    \end{align*}
    
    implying the statement of the lemma.
nodes.section: 5.2 Definition and existence of standard flags
nodes.statement_short: Union bound

nodes.name: Case of disjoint cliques
nodes.statement:
Assume that $X_1\cap X_2 = \varnothing$. By \cref{lem:Claim_2}, there exists two sets $M_1, M_2\subseteq X_1 \ast X_2$ of edges satisfying $|M_2(x_1)| \le 1$ for any $x_1 \in X_1$ and $|M_1(x_2)| \le 1$ for any $x_2 \in X_2$  that are, respectively, all colored with color $c_1$ and $c_2$.

    
    If $c_1\ne c_2$, let us assume that $M_1$ is non-empty and pick some arbitrary edge $\{v_1,v_2\}\in M_1$ with $v_1\in X_1$ and $v_2\in X_2$. Applying \cref{lem:Claim_2} to $X_2$ and $v_1$ implies that that
    \[
        M_1 \supseteq v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1)).
    \]
    with $|M_2(v_1)| \le 1$.
    Since $|M_1(x_2)|\le 1$ for all $x_2\in X_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2}, it follows that there can exist at most one additional edge in $M_1$ that is not in $v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1))$, namely $\{M_2(v_1), z\}$ for some $z\in X_1\setminus v_1$. This however would likewise imply that $M_1 \supseteq z \ast (X_2 \setminus M_2(z))$ with $|M_2(z)| \le 1$, contradicting that $|M_1| \leq |X_2|$. Hence either $M_1 = \emptyset$ or
    \[
        M_1 = v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1))
    \]
    and by symmetry either $M_2 = \emptyset$ or 
    \[
        M_2 = (X_1\setminus M_1(v_2)) \ast v_2,
    \]
    for some $v_2 \in X_2$.
    It follows that there exists $v_ \in X_1$ and $v_2 \in X_2$ such that
    
    \begin{equation*}
        (X_1\setminus\{v_1\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v_2 \}) \subseteq X_1 \ast X_2 \setminus (M_1 \cup M_2)
    \end{equation*}
    
    and all edges in $(X_1\setminus\{v_1\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v_2 \})$ need to have the same color $c_3$ distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2} and symmetry. Then however, since we are assuming that $c_1 \neq c_2$, we get the contradiction that $p(\hat K_{3,3}; F) > 0$.
    
    If $c_1=c_2$, then $M_1 = M_2$ needs to be a matching by symmetry and $(X_1\ast X_2)\setminus (M_1\cup M_2)$ is again monochromatic with a color distinct from $c_1=c_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Case of disjoint cliques

nodes.name: Apply Claim 5
nodes.statement: Assume that $X_1\cap X_2 = \varnothing$. By \cref{lem:Claim_2}, there exists two sets $M_1, M_2\subseteq X_1 \ast X_2$ of edges satisfying $|M_2(x_1)| \le 1$ for any $x_1 \in X_1$ and $|M_1(x_2)| \le 1$ for any $x_2 \in X_2$  that are, respectively, all colored with color $c_1$ and $c_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Claim 5.5 to get edge sets $M_1,M_2$

nodes.name: Different colors give a $\hat K_{3,3}$ configuration
nodes.statement:
If $c_1\ne c_2$, let us assume that $M_1$ is non-empty and pick some arbitrary edge $\{v_1,v_2\}\in M_1$ with $v_1\in X_1$ and $v_2\in X_2$. Applying \cref{lem:Claim_2} to $X_2$ and $v_1$ implies that that
    \[
        M_1 \supseteq v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1)).
    \]
    with $|M_2(v_1)| \le 1$.
    Since $|M_1(x_2)|\le 1$ for all $x_2\in X_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2}, it follows that there can exist at most one additional edge in $M_1$ that is not in $v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1))$, namely $\{M_2(v_1), z\}$ for some $z\in X_1\setminus v_1$. This however would likewise imply that $M_1 \supseteq z \ast (X_2 \setminus M_2(z))$ with $|M_2(z)| \le 1$, contradicting that $|M_1| \leq |X_2|$. Hence either $M_1 = \emptyset$ or
    \[
        M_1 = v_1 \ast (X_2\setminus M_2(v_1))
    \]
    and by symmetry either $M_2 = \emptyset$ or 
    \[
        M_2 = (X_1\setminus M_1(v_2)) \ast v_2,
    \]
    for some $v_2 \in X_2$.
    It follows that there exists $v_ \in X_1$ and $v_2 \in X_2$ such that
    
    \begin{equation*}
        (X_1\setminus\{v_1\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v_2 \}) \subseteq X_1 \ast X_2 \setminus (M_1 \cup M_2)
    \end{equation*}
    
    and all edges in $(X_1\setminus\{v_1\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v_2 \})$ need to have the same color $c_3$ distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2} and symmetry. Then however, since we are assuming that $c_1 \neq c_2$, we get the contradiction that $p(\hat K_{3,3}; F) > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Different colors give a $\hat K_{3,3}$ configuration

nodes.name: Equal colors give a matching
nodes.statement: If $c_1=c_2$, then $M_1 = M_2$ needs to be a matching by symmetry and $(X_1\ast X_2)\setminus (M_1\cup M_2)$ is again monochromatic with a color distinct from $c_1=c_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal colors give a matching

nodes.name: Cliques meeting in one vertex
nodes.statement: Assume now that $|X_1\cap X_2| = \{v\}$ and pick an arbitrary $w \in X_2 \setminus X_1$. Then $\{v,w\}$ has color $c_2$ and so all edges in $w \ast (X_1 \setminus \{v\})$ have the same color $c_3$ distinct from $c_2$ by \cref{lem:Claim_2}. By symmetry, the same argument is true for edges going from any $w\in X_1\setminus X_2$ to the set $X_2\setminus \{v\}$ with the color being distinct from $c_1$. Since $(X_1\setminus \{v\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v\})$ is a complete bipartite graph, the symmetry also implies that the color $c_3$ is the same for each choice of $w$, so that all edges in $(X_1\setminus \{v\})\ast (X_2\setminus \{v\})$ have the same color $c_3$ distinct from $c_1$ and $c_2$. Finally, if $c_1 \ne c_2$, we would get a contradiction to the assumption that $p(\hat K_{3,3};F) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Cliques meeting in one vertex

nodes.name: Two common vertices are impossible
nodes.statement: Finally, if $|X_1\cap X_2| \ge 2$, then there exist $v_1, v_2 \in X_1\cap X_2$ and the edge $\{v_1, v_2\}$ therefore has both colors $c_1$ and $c_2$, implying that $c_1 = c_2$. By assumption $X_1 \neq X_2$, so there exists $v\in X_1\Delta X_2$. Let us w.l.o.g. say that $v\in X_2$. Then, for each $w \in X_1 \cap X_2$, of which there are at least two, the edge $\{v,w\}$ as color $c_1$, contradicting \cref{lem:Claim_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Two common vertices are impossible

nodes.name: No monochromatic triangle through a clique vertex
nodes.statement_short: No monochromatic triangle through a clique vertex

nodes.name: Assume a monochromatic triangle through a clique vertex
nodes.statement:
We begin with the proof of the second claim.
    Assume $v_1, v_2, v_3\in V(E)$ with $v_1\in\mathcal{X}_F$ forms a monochromatic triangle in $E_F$. Denote the color of this triangle by $c_\triangle \in [c]$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a monochromatic triangle through a clique vertex

nodes.name: Exclude degenerate cases via Claims 5
nodes.statement:
The case 
    $|\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}|= 2$ is not possible \cref{lem:Claim_4} contradicts the case that $v_1,v_2,v_3 \in \mathcal{X}_F$ and \cref{lem:Claim_2} contradicts the case where one of $v_1,v_2,v_3$ is in $Y$. Note that we cannot have two of the vertices in $Y$ as $E_F$ does not have loops in $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: Exclude degenerate cases via Claims 5.5 and 5.6

nodes.name: Find an $\mathcal H(2,1,0)$ copy
nodes.statement_short: Find an $\mathcal H(2,1,0)$ copy

nodes.name: Large cliques would lie in $Y$, contradiction
nodes.statement:
Now let us prove the first claim.
    Assume that $E_F$ contains an embedding of $K_{\max(c+1,6)}^{c'}$ at vertices $v_1,\dots,v_{\max(c+1,6)}$ for some $c' \in [c]$. By the just established claim, $v_i \notin \mathcal{X}_F$ for all $1 \leq i \leq \max(c+1,6)$. This however implies that $Y$ would contain a copy of $K^{c'}_{\operatorname{max(c+1,6)}}$, giving us a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Large cliques would lie in $Y$, contradiction

nodes.name: Lower bound triangle density by cliques
nodes.statement:
Because $E_F$ without its loops contains no $K^i_{\operatorname{max(c+1,6)}}$, $v(E)$ is bounded independently of $n_1$. The elements of $\mathcal{X}_F$ intersect pairwise in at most one point. Therefore, 
\begin{equation} p(\hat K_3; F)
    \ge
    \frac{\sum_{X\in\mathcal{X}_F}\binom{X}{3}}{\binom{n_1}{3}} \geq ....
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound triangle density by cliques

nodes.name: Too few cliques contradict the Ramsey upper bound
nodes.statement_short: Too few cliques contradict the Ramsey upper bound

nodes.name: Hence exactly $R_{c-1}(3)-1$ cliques
nodes.statement:
Since $E_F[\mathcal{X}_F]$ is triangle-free, we cannot have $|\mathcal{X}_F| \geq R_{c-1}(3)$ and therefore
$|\mathcal{X}_F|= R_{c-1}(3)-1$ follows.
nodes.statement_short: Hence exactly $R_{c-1}(3)-1$ cliques

nodes.name: Exclude leftover vertices via Claim 5
nodes.statement: To prove that $Y_F=\varnothing$, assume that there existed $v\in Y_F$. Then, since we know that $|\mathcal{X}_F| = R_{c-1}(3)-1$, there needs to exist two distinct $w_1,w_2\in \mathcal{X}_F$ so that $v,w_1,w_2$ is a monochromatic triangle in $E_F$. This however would contradict \cref{lem:standard_has_partition}. Therefore, $E_F\in\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Exclude leftover vertices via Claim 5.7

nodes.name: Clique sizes are balanced
nodes.statement: Finally, assume now that the bound in \cref{eq:first_bound_on_cliques} was not fulfilled, say because $|X|$ was too large. Then, we could bound $p(\hat K_3;F)$ just as in \cref{eq:first_bound_on_triangle_density} and would similarly arrive at a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Clique sizes are balanced

nodes.name: Cliques cover $V(F)$
nodes.statement: First, let us note that $\mathcal{X}_F = \{X_1,\dots, X_{r}\}$ is a covering of $V(F)$ by \cref{lem:standard_is_Ramsey}. The same therefore holds for $C_i = \mathscr W \cap X_i$ with respect to $W$.
nodes.statement_short: Cliques cover $V(F)$

nodes.name: Split failure into three events
nodes.statement:
We can lower bound the probability $P$ of $\mathscr W$ having the desired properties by
    
    \begin{equation} P \geq 1 - P_1 - P_2 - P_3,
    \end{equation}
    
    where $P_1$ denotes that probability that the $C_i$ do not form a partition of $\mathscr W$, $P_2$ the probability that there exists $i,j$ s.t. $|C_i| / |C_j| \le 1- \varepsilon_4$, and $P_3$ the probability that there does not exist an embedding $\varphi$ with the desired properties conditioned on $C_i$ being a partition of $\mathscr W$.
nodes.statement_short: Split failure into three events

nodes.name: Injectivity probability
nodes.statement:
Writing $P_I$ for the probability that a random function $[n_2] \to [n_1]$ is injective, we note that 
    \[
        \mathbb P[I] = \frac{n_1!}{(n_1-n_2)! \, n_1^{n_2}} \geq 1 - \varepsilon_4
    \]    
    for \whiteboxedchar{$n_1$ sufficiently large}.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity probability

nodes.name: Bound $P_1$ by Boole's inequality
nodes.statement_short: Bound $P_1$ by Boole's inequality

nodes.name: Bound $P_2$ by Chernoff-Hoeffding
nodes.statement_short: Bound $P_2$ by Chernoff-Hoeffding

nodes.name: Bound $P_3$ via the majority matchings
nodes.statement_short: Bound $P_3$ via the majority matchings

nodes.name: Combine the bounds
nodes.statement: Combining these bounds establishes that  $P \geq 1 - \varepsilon_4$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the bounds

nodes.name: Random $n_2$-sets embed w
nodes.statement:
If $\mathscr U$ is a uniform random subsets of $G$ of size $n_2$, and for each $F\in\mathcal{F}^\varnothing_{n_1}$, $\mathscr W_F$ is a uniform random subset of $F$ of size $n_2$ then we get
    
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P[G[\mathscr U]\text{ embeds into some $\mathcal{L}^{(c)}_{\operatorname{ex}}$}]
        &\ge
        \sum_{\substack{F\in\mathcal{F}_{n_1}^\varnothing\\ F\text{ is $\varepsilon_1$-standard}}} \mathbb P[G[\mathscr W_F]\text{ embeds into } E_F] \, p(F;G) \\
        &\ge(1-\varepsilon_4)^2 \ge 1-2\varepsilon_4,
    \end{align*}
    
    where the first inequality follows by \cref{lemma:double_counting}, the second inequality follow from \cref{lem:standard_has_uniform_subgraph}, \cref{lem:Claim_1} and \boxedchar{A4}, and the last inequality simply omits the quadratic term. Note that the same also holds if $\mathscr U$ is of size $n_2 +1$ and $n_2 + 2$, assuming \whiteboxedchar{$n_1$, $n_2$, and $\varepsilon_3$} are adjusted accordingly.
nodes.statement_short: Random $n_2$-sets embed w.h.p. (Lemmas 3.1, 5.4, 5.9)

nodes.name: Random $W$ and two random vertices; partition into five even
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathscr W$ be an  $n_2$-sized subset of $G$ chosen uniformly at random and let $\mathscr P_1$ and $\mathscr P_2$ be two vertices in $V(G)$ also chosen uniformly at random. Note that $\mathscr W$, $\mathscr P_1$, and $\mathscr P_2$ are independent and let the following five events partition our probability space
    
    \begin{align*}
        I_1 &= \{\mathscr P_1\in \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \in \mathscr W\}, \\
        I_2 &= \{\mathscr P_1\in \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \notin \mathscr W\}, \\
        I_3 &= \{\mathscr P_1\notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \in \mathscr W\}, \\
        I_4 &= \{\mathscr P_1\notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_1 = \mathscr P_2\}, \text{ and} \\
        I_5 &= \{\mathscr P_1\notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_2 \notin \mathscr W\land \mathscr P_1 \ne \mathscr P_2\} .
    \end{align*}
    Then $\mathscr W \cup \{\mathscr P_1, \mathscr P_2\}$ is a uniform random $n_2$-sized set when conditioned on $I_1$, uniform random $(n_2+1)$-sized set when conditioned on $I_2,I_3$ or $I_4$ and a random $(n_2+2)$-sized subset when conditioned on $I_5$.
nodes.statement_short: Random $W$ and two random vertices; partition into five events

nodes.name: Combine over the five events
nodes.statement:
It follows that
    \begin{align*}
    &\mathbb P[\mathscr W \cup \{\mathscr P_1, \mathscr P_2\}\text{ embeds into some }\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}]\\
    &=
    \sum_{i=1,\dots,5} \mathbb P[(\mathscr W \cup \{\mathscr P_1, \mathscr P_2\} \text{ embeds into some } \mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}) \text{ and } I_i \text{ holds} \} \ge 1 - 10\varepsilon_4
    \end{align*}
    due to the oberservation at the beginning of this proof.
nodes.statement_short: Combine over the five events

nodes.name: Fix a good set $W$
nodes.statement_short: Fix a good set $W$

nodes.name: Uniqueness of $E$
nodes.statement: When \whiteboxedchar{$n_2$ is sufficiently large}, there exists exactly one $E\in\mathcal{L}_{\operatorname{ex}}^{(c)}$ into which $G[W]$ embeds, proving the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of $E$

nodes.name: Small $F_i$ would force too many triangles
nodes.statement:
First, note that

nodes.statement: Let us sketch the argument that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}^\varnothing \cong \mathcal{A}^\varnothing / \langle \mathcal{H}\rangle$. There is an algebra homomorphism $\pi: \mathcal{A}^\varnothing \to \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}^\varnothing$ defined by mapping a flag $F\in \mathcal{F}$ to $F$ if $F\in \mathcal{F}^\varnothing_{\mathcal{H}}$ and otherwise to 0, see \cite{Razborov_2007} Definition 4 and Theorem 2.6. Clearly, it is surjective and $\langle \mathcal{H} \rangle$ is in its kernel. To see that its kernel is exactly $\langle \mathcal{H} \rangle$ we notice that if $\pi(f)=0$ then $\pi(f)$ may be written as a linear combination of elements of $\mathcal{K}^\varnothing_{\mathcal{H}}$. But we can pull back this linear combination to a linear combination of $\mathcal{K}^\varnothing$ and then it follows that $f$ is in $\langle \mathcal{H}\rangle$.

Let $t_v^{(b)}$ and $t_v^{(a)}$ therefore denote the number of monochromatic triangles incident to $v$ in $G$ \emph{before} and \emph{after} recoloring. We have
    
    \begin{equation} t_v^{(a)} \leq \binom{|V_{i^\ast}|}{2}   + |E^\ast| + |V^\ast| \, n

nodes.name: Basic lower bound on triangles before recoloring

     \sum_{j\le k}
        G[v,V_j,E(\{j,k\})] \, G[v,V_k, E(\{j,k\})]
        \cdot\begin{cases}
            \frac{1}{2} \text{ if } j=k \\
            1 \text{ otherwise }
        \end{cases}-\varepsilon_5n^2
        -r n,
    \end{equation}
    
    where the term $\varepsilon_5n^2$ accounts for $|E^*|$, the term $-r n$ 
    arises from the fact that we are 
    overcounting, and the coefficient $1/2$ from the fact that
    \[
        \binom{G[v,V_j, E(j)]}{2}
        \ge
        \frac{1}{2} \, G[v,V_j, E(j)]^2 - n.
    \]
    Our task is therefore to lower bound
    \cref{eq:basic_lower_bound} and compare it to the upper bound of $t_v^{(a)}$.

nodes.name: Minimum excess at distance $x$
nodes.statement:
We want to compute for a given $1>x>0$
\begin{align*}
    \min_{\min_{s\in R_n}\|\max(\kappa-s,0)\|_1=x} Q_n(\kappa)-\varsigma_n
\end{align*}
where $\kappa$ ranges over vectors in the standard simplex $\Delta^r$. By symmetry we may assume that 
\[
    s = \frac{1}{n}\left(\lceil \frac{n}{r}\rceil, \dots, \lceil \frac{n}{r}\rceil, \lfloor \frac{n}{r}\rfloor, \dots, \lfloor \frac{n}{r}\rfloor\right)
\]
and that $\kappa$ exceeds $s$ on the first $l$ coordinates. 
In this case, we find that the global minimum is at most $x^3/r^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimum excess at distance $x$

nodes.name: Reduce to $E^*\subseteq E_0$
nodes.statement:
Let us show that we now may assume that

\begin{equation}
    E^\ast \subseteq E_0 .
\end{equation}

For any $(x,y)\in E^\ast$ with $x\in V_i$ and $y\in V_j$ we know that $i \neq j$ by \cref{lem:Claim_10}.
Let us show that $G[\{x,y\}\cup W]$ does not embed into $E$ so that $(x,y) \in E_0$. If it were embeddable, then $x$ would get assigned to the same vertex in $E$ as the class $C_i$ and $y$ to the same vertex as $C_j$ because the edges in $x\ast C_i$ and $y\ast C_j$ are monochromatic
with the loop color of $E$  by \cref{lem:Claim_10}.
By assumption though, $G(\{x,y\})\ne E(\{i,j\})$, which contradicts the embedding.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $E^*\subseteq E_0$
